text:
3.1 Downloading packages
Packages in R are collections of functions, compiled code, and sample data. They are located in a directory called “library” in the R environment. By default R has a set of packages installed which include packages such as base, datasets and stats. Most of the functions you have used so far are stored in the base package. The package to which a function belongs can be seen from the function’s help page next to the function name in the top left corner inside curly brackets { }.
To get the list of all the packages installed, you can run:

library()

Packages which are not part of the base build need to be loaded explicitly by the user. The Packages tab typically located at the bottom right in RStudio (next to the Help tab) shows the packages that have been installed but not loaded. The command:

search()

prints a list of the packages that are currently loaded in the R environment. If you run it, you should see that most packages are not preloaded. library(<package name>) can be used to load an installed package for use. For example

library("tools")

loads the tools package to the R environment. If you run search() again, the package should show up.
To use additional packages, you first need to install them. There are three main ways to install R packages:

From CRAN (recommended and easiest): You can install any package directly from the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN) by running this command in the R console:

install.packages("package_name")

Replace package_name with the name of the package you want to install (you don’t need to know any packages now, we’ll introduce some later. If you want, you can search for interesting packages at https://rdrr.io/.)
Manual installation:Download the package source file (e.g., .zip or .tar.gz) and install manually. The general syntax is:

install.packages("path/to/package_file.zip", repos = NULL, type = "source")

where

"path/to/package_file.zip" is replaced with your local path to the source file.
repos: a character vector specifying the URL of the repositories to use.
type: character, indicating the type of package to download and install (see ?install.packages for more).

From GitHub or other online repositories (using devtools or remotes):
Sometimes packages are available only on GitHub or developments versions (early versions) of the packages are hosted there. You can install these using the devtools or remotes packages:

# First install devtools or remotes if not already installed
install.packages("devtools")  
# Then install the package from GitHub
devtools::install_github("username/repository")

Replace "username/repository" with the correct GitHub repo path.

6.1 For-loops
In real data analysis, we often work with data frames that have many variables (columns) and many observations (rows). Suppose we want to compute the mean of each variable. One way to do this is:

mean(df[,1])
mean(df[,2])
mean(df[,3])
mean(df[,4])
mean(df[,5])

… and so on. But this quickly becomes tedious and error-prone, especially if your data has hundreds or even thousands of columns.
Fortunately, R provides built-in functions for many common tasks, such as colMeans(df), which returns the means of each numeric variable in a data frame and which we’ll introduce at the end of this Module. Typically, you often need something more flexible, like computing multiple summary statistics or performing a custom operation on each column simultaneously. This is where for-loops (for) come in.

Why for-loops?
A for-loop allows the user to automate repetitive tasks: we can write code once, and run it over many objects, adapting to the task performed at each step. This avoids copy-pasting repetitive lines of code over and over, and makes the code easier to read, modify and reuse. In other words, you should be thinking about for-loops (or similar methods) whenever:

You need to perform a certain operation or a set of operations (such as computing many statistics) across all variables or observations in a matrix or a data frame.
You need to perform a certain task multiple times or for a number of different objects in a certain sequence.
You are working with dynamically sized data sets.



for-loop syntax
The basic syntax for writing for-loops in R is as follows:

for (variable in sequence) {
  # code to execute at each step
}

Where

variable: a syntactical name for a variable which changes in the loop, such as i.
sequence: an expression that evaluates to a vector, such as 1:10, 1:length(x), or 1:ncol(df).

That is, we want to iterate over some values, such as numbers from 1 to 10, indices of a vector, or the column indices of a data frame. For example:

for(i in 1:10){
  print(i)
}

[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 3
[1] 4
[1] 5
[1] 6
[1] 7
[1] 8
[1] 9
[1] 10


Loops over the numbers from 1 to 10, and the loop prints each of these numbers. Similarly we can create a vector of which elements we loop over:

for(i in seq(1, 10, 2)){
  print(i)
}

[1] 1
[1] 3
[1] 5
[1] 7
[1] 9




Example: for-loop with a data frame
Suppose we want to compute the mean of each column in a data frame df. Instead of writing one line per variable, we can loop over all columns using ncol(df) (the number of columns in df):

for(i in 1:ncol(df)){
  mean(df[, i])
}

We can also build a summary table of a data set by computing different statistics per column. For example, to compute a summary of the numeric variables of penguins data, filtered for female penguins on the Dream island (using subset()):

df <- as.data.frame(subset(
  penguins, 
  subset = island == "Dream" & sex == "female", 
  select = c(bill_length_mm, bill_depth_mm, flipper_length_mm, body_mass_g)
  )
)

summary <- data.frame("mean"    = vector("numeric", length = ncol(df)), 
                     "median"  = vector("numeric", length = ncol(df)),
                     "minimum" = vector("numeric", length = ncol(df)),
                     "maximum" = vector("numeric", length = ncol(df)))

rownames(summary) <- colnames(df)

for(i in 1:ncol(df)){
  summary[i,] <- c(
    mean(df[,i]), 
    median(df[,i]), 
    min(df[,i]), 
    max(df[,i])
    )
}

summary

                        mean median minimum maximum
bill_length_mm      42.29672   42.5    32.1    58.0
bill_depth_mm       17.60164   17.8    15.5    19.4
flipper_length_mm  190.01639  190.0   178.0   202.0
body_mass_g       3446.31148 3450.0  2700.0  4150.0


This loop constructs a table with four summary statistics for each variable selected.


Nested for-loops
Suppose you have two variables over which you need to loop. In other words, for every value of the first variable, you want to iterate over a second set of values. This situation arises, for example, when you want to visit every element of a matrix. In such cases, you can use nested loops, which are loops inside another loop:

A = matrix(c(1:6), nrow = 3, ncol = 2, byrow = T)
A

     [,1] [,2]
[1,]    1    2
[2,]    3    4
[3,]    5    6

for(i in 1:nrow(A)){
  for(j in 1:ncol(A)){
    print(A[i,j])
  }
}

[1] 1
[1] 2
[1] 3
[1] 4
[1] 5
[1] 6


The nested loop above goes through each element in a \(3 \times 2\) matrix A, which contains the numbers from 1 to 6. The loop indices are \(i\) (rows) and \(j\) (columns). For example, when \(i = 2\), the inner loop runs from \(j=1\) to \(j=2\), because A has only two columns. In fact, for each value of \(i\), that is, for each value of the outer loop, the inner loop runs over the number of columns in A.
You can nest as many loops as you like, but deep nesting (more than two nested loops) is generally discouraged because it makes code harted to read and maintain.

6.2 While-loop
Above, we learned that a for-loop is a handy tool to reduce repetition in code when we have a certain known range or sequence over which we want to loop. However, sometimes it is the case that we simply do not know beforehand how many times we need to repeat something. What if we need to keep on doing something until a certain condition is met? That’s when we use a while-loop.

Why while-loops?
A while-loop is useful when you want to repeat a task an unknown number of times, but stop as soon as some pre-specified logical condition is satisfied. In other words, while-loops keep on doing something until a certain condition (or its opposite) holds.
while-loops are typically used to:

Simulate a process until a threshold is crossed.
Create iterative methods that converge to a solution (such as numerical optimization methods).
Searching for or waiting for a certain (optimal) value.
Debugging or testing until an error condition is met.



while-loop syntax

while (condition) {
  # code to repeat until condition is no longer true
}

Note that the condition is TRUE at first, and the while-loop runs until the condition is FALSE. R checks the condition before each iteration, i.e. at the beginning of the code-block. If the condition is TRUE, it runs through the code-block, otherwise it stops the loop.


Example: rolling a die
Suppose that for whatever reason, you want to simulate rolling a die until you get a six, and you want to compute the number of rolls. Before you start rolling, you do not know how many rolls it will take as it is random. You can use a while-loop to simulate this:

set.seed(2025)
roll <- 0
count <- 0

while(roll != 6){
  roll  <- sample(1:6, 1)
  count <- count + 1
}

print(paste("It took: ", count, " rolls to get a six!"))

[1] "It took:  6  rolls to get a six!"


The above code simulates one die roll at a time and continues until a 6 appears, that is, when roll != 6 is no longer TRUE. It keeps track of the number of rolls in the count variable, which, in this simulation, turned out to be 6 (you’ll learn a lot more about simulation in the next Module).


An important caution regarding infinite loops
When constructing while-loops, keep in mind that in the case that the condition never becomes false, the loop will never stop. In other words, if the condition remains TRUE throughout the loop, it will run forever. Such a situation is known as an infinite loop, and it can easily happen with while-loops, if you forget this. So for example:

while (TRUE) {
  print("Stuck in a loop....")
}

will never stop printing the words “Stuck in a loop…”.
Infinite loops use up system resources like CPU and memory without ever finishing, and it makes your R session unresponsive or even cause it to crash. You may then have to force a restart which can potentially cause unsaved changes to lose. You can avoid infinite loops by:

Making sure that the condition in your while loop will eventually become FALSE. Usually this means updating a variable that affects the condition inside the loop.
Use counters or safeguards that limit the number of iterations with an additional condition (e.g., count < max_iterations).
Test your loop with simpler cases or print debugging messages inside the loop to verify progress.
If an infinite loop happens, you can manually stop it by clicking on the STOP button in the top right corner of the console in RStudio, or pressing the ESC key or Ctrl + C.

4 Probability distribution functions in R
In this module, we will cover core ideas in probability, simulations and probability distributions. Now that we know to read, transform, and summarize data in R, the next steps as statisticians-in-training is to understand what the data tells us. To do that, we must acknowledge a central fact: all data we come across is uncertain. It varies due to chance, and we need to understand probability to understand it.
We begin by learning how to simulate random data from common probability distributions like the normal, uniform and binomial distributions. Simulation provides a controlled environment where we know the underlying rules. This is powerful, because it allows us to safely test ideas, validate methods, and understand how randomness affects our conclusions.
Next, we’ll look at how to perform probability calculations in R using built-in functions. These tools help us answer questions like: what’s the probability that I’ll have to wait 6 minutes for a train tomorrow morning? Or, what value corresponds to the 90th percentile of the distribution of test scores?
From there, we turn to conditional execution: a fundamental programming skill that allows code to behave differently depending on the circumstances. Think of it as: if something is true, do this; otherwise, do something else. This enables more responsive and intelligent analysis pipelines.
We’ll then introduce user-defined functions as a way to automate tasks and write cleaner, more flexible code. You’re already familiar with using built-in functions like mean() or sum(), and now you’ll learn to write your own!
Finally, we’ll bring everything to life with visualizations. Instead of just writing code and printing long lists of numbers, we’ll learn how to visualize the same information into a much more human-digestible form with histograms, probability density function plots, and other creative visual summaries.
In R, there are built-in functions for a variety of probability distributions. For these distributions, R has a consistent system of functions for different use cases. We’ll first briefly describe these functions, before moving on to the distributions themselves, to highlight that they are common to all distributions and hence understanding when and why they are used is key to learning. The system consists of the following four functions, where * is replaced with the desired distribution abbreviation (see below) and the parameters associated with that distribution:
So, all of the functions are intimately related to probability distributions and/or concepts derived from them. After the conceptual introduction, let’s next dive deeper with concrete examples! We’ll cover the following distributions here, but all of the above functions work exactly the same for the different built-in distributions in R (Note: most of these are included in the stats package which is contained in the base R installation).
You can find a list of distributions and their corresponding packages here.

title: 3  Probability, simulations, and distributions
text:
4.1 Normal distribution
Let’s start with the normal distribution, which is arguably the most important distribution in statistics. It describes a continuous random variable that is symmetrically distributed around its mean, or the expected value. Surprisingly many real-world phenomena are normally distributed, heights and weights of people, scores on the Finnish Matriculation Examination, measurement errors in real-life experiments, and a whole lot more, at least when the sample size is large enough. In fact, by the central limit theorem, if you add together enough random variables that themselves are not normal, their sum begins to look normal as the sample size grows.
The normal distribution is also called the bell curve due to its shape, and it is defined by two parameters only:

Mean \(\mu\): the center of the distribution.
Standard deviation \(\sigma\): controls how spread out the distribution is.

The normal distribution’s probability density function is given by:
\[
f(x;\mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} \exp \left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right),
\]
and a random variable \(X\) that is normally distributed is usually denoted by \(X \sim \text{N}(\mu,\sigma^2)\). A variety of normal distributions are visualized below. Can you see how different parameter values affect the shape of the distribution?









Next we’ll demonstrate through examples how to use the different functions introduced earlier with normal distributions, for which the abbreviation norm is used (i.e., rnorm, dnorm, pnorm, qnorm).

Example: pouring coffee in the morning
Assume that the amount of coffee you pour into your mug (or the water container of the brewing machine) each morning follows a normal distribution. Your mug can hold 265 ml so you aim for \(\mu = 250\) millilitres (ml), but in practice sometimes you’re in a rush and pour less and sometimes you’re a bit distracted and pour a bit more. Assume further that your pours are quite precise, with a small standard deviation, say \(\sigma = 10\). This means that on most days, you pour between 240-260 ml, and only occasionally pour as little as 220 ml or overfill to 270 ml.
The function used to generate random draws from the normal distribution is rnorm, which takes three parameters: n (number of draws), mean (\(\mu\)), and sd (standard deviation, \(\sigma\)). For example:

rnorm(n = 5, mean = 0, sd = 1)

would return five realizations of the standard normal distribution which is the normal distribution with \(\mu = 0\) and \(\sigma = 1\). Increasing the mean shifts the distribution to higher values, while increasing the standard deviation spreads the values out more, that is, we get values that are more dispersed around the mean.
Let’s generate a full week’s worth of coffee pours:

rnorm(n = 7, mean = 250, sd = 10)

[1] 236.2366 247.1174 237.4943 239.2605 266.3576 237.7714 268.1749


That seems reasonable!
Let’s next see how we can use pnorm to evaluate how likely a certain coffee pour is. Recall that the p* family of distribution functions returns the cumulative probability that a random value is less than or equal to a given value. This means that we can use it to compute the probability that a given pour is between 240 and 260 ml. Given that a coffee pour is distributed as \(X \sim \text{N}(\mu = 250, \sigma = 10)\), then the probability that we are after is given by
\[
\text{Pr}(250 \leq X \leq 260) = \int_{240}^{260} f_X(x) dx = \int_0^{260} f_X(x) dx - \int_0^{240} f_X(x) dx,
\]
where \(X\) denotes a single coffee pour as a random variable and \(f_X(x)\) is the density function given above. The CDF allows us to compute the probability up to a given value, so the desired probability is given by the difference:

pnorm(260, mean = 250, sd = 10) - pnorm(240, mean = 250, sd = 10)

[1] 0.6826895


As noted earlier, you are a rather precise coffee pourer!
In a similar manner, you could be interested in “cutoff” values such that only 5% of your pours fall below or above them. That is, what is the interval that contains 90% of your pours. In R, this is obtained via the qnorm:

qnorm(0.05, mean = 250, sd = 10)

[1] 233.5515

qnorm(0.95, mean = 250, sd = 10)

[1] 266.4485


How about dnorm? Well, for example, we use it to plot the following (see the last section of this Module to learn to produce it!)

x <- seq(220, 280, 0.1)
dens <- dnorm(x, mean = 250, sd = 10)

plot(x, dens, type = "l", main = "Pouring Coffee",
     ylab = "Density", xlab = "ml")
polygon(c(240, seq(240, 260, 0.1), 260),
        c(0, dnorm(seq(240, 260, 0.1), mean = 250, sd = 10), 0),
        col = "skyblue")








In summary, our example shows that the functionalities provide:

rnorm: simulate random coffee pourings
pnorm: get the probability that you pour at most a certain amount of coffee
qnorm: get the pour amount below which (or above which) a certain percentage of values fall.
dnorm: get how typical a specific pour is, or for visualization!

title: 3  Probability, simulations, and distributions
text:
4.2 Uniform distribution
Now we’ll turn to the uniform distribution, which is one of the simplest continuous probability distributions. A random variable that is uniformly distributed is equally likely to take any value within a certain range. This means that the probability of the variable falling anywhere within this interval is the same, that is, there is no bias toward any particular value. (In contrast, a normally distributed random variable is most likely to take values near the mean.)
The uniform distribution is a natural choice to model phenomena where the set of values the random variable can take is limited to a range, and we have no reason to expect any of those values to be more likely than another. Next, using an example, we’ll demonstrate how to use the R functions associated with the uniform distribution: runif, dunif, punif, and qunif.

Example: Waiting time at a train station
Imagine that you take the train to your work or university every morning. The train you are trying to catch leaves at 8:00, and you tend to arrive at the station at an unpredictable time around then (randomly). There are also trains that leave at 7:50 and 8:10, meaning that if you arrive up to 10 minutes early or late, you don’t have to wait at all. This means that your waiting time for the next train (from the time you arrive at the station) is uniformly distributed between 0 and 10 minutes, because your arrival time is uncertain.
The uniform distribution is defined by two parameters:

Minimum value: denoted \(a\), the smallest possible value. In our example \(a = 0\) minutes of waiting.
Maximum value: denoted \(b\), the largest possible value. In our example \(b= 10\) minutes of waiting.

The probability density function of the uniform distribution is constant between \(a\) and \(b\):
\[
f(x; a,b) = \begin{cases} \frac{1}{b-a} \,\, &\mathrm{for a \leq x \leq b} \\ 0 \,\, &\mathrm{otherwise} \end{cases}.
\]
This means that the density is flat: every value in \([a,b]\) is equally likely:









You’ll learn about the uniform distribution and its properties more in your other statistics classes.
We can generate random waiting times with R using the function runif:

runif(n = 5, min = 0, max = 10)

[1] 6.365602 3.590474 5.244644 5.112901 9.473216


Where n is, again, the number of draws, and min and max are the minimum and maximum values introduced earlier. Similarly, we have:

punif(q, min, max): returns the cumulative probability \(P(X\leq q)\), i.e., the probability that the waiting time is at most \(q\).
qunif(p, min, max): returns the quantile value for probability \(p\), i.e., the waiting time below which \(p \times 100\%\) of waiting times fall.
dunif(x, min, max): returns the value of the density function at point \(x\), which for uniform distribution is constant between minimum and maximum.

Given that our example is very simple \(X \sim \text{Uniform}(0,10)\), we notice that the probability that the waiting time is less than, say, 4 minutes is:
\[
P(X \leq 4) = \frac{4 - 0}{10 - 0} = \frac{4}{10} = 0.4
\]
and we get this in R by:

punif(4, min = 0, max = 10)

[1] 0.4

# 40% chance that you wait at most 4 minutes

Similarly, we can ask that what is the time \(t\) such that 90% of the waiting times are less than \(t\)? Using the quantile function we get:

qunif(0.9, min = 0, max = 10)

[1] 9


And we can verify it by computing:
\[
t = a + p\times (b-a) = 0 + 0.9 \times 10 = 9.
\]
In summary:

runif: simulate waiting times
punif: get the probability that you wait at most a certain amount of time
qunif: get the threshold for waiting times below which a certain percentage of values fall.
dunif: get the (constant) density.

title: 3  Probability, simulations, and distributions
text:
4.3 Binomial distribution
While normal and uniform distributions describe a continuous random variable, we’ll now turn to discrete random variables. Discrete variables assume only a fixed set of possible outcomes, with the simplest example being a binary random variable that can only take one of two possible values. As a single draw (\(n = 1\), see below) , e.g. a coin flip, a binary variable follows a Bernoulli distribution and takes on a value of 1 with probability \(p\), and 0 with probability \(1-p\). In practice, 1 and 0 can mean anything, this is just the conventional way to code a binary variable. Typically, 1 is called a “success” and 0 a “failure”, but in practice their meaning depends entirely on the context.
The Bernoulli distribution is a special case of the binomial distribution, which describes the number of successes in \(n\) independent repetitions of a Bernoulli trial. A random variable that follows a binomial distribution is denoted \(X \sim \mathrm{Binomial}(n,p)\) and is completely described by the parameters:

n: number of draws/trials.
p: probability of a success.

And where \(X\) denotes the number of successes.
The binomial probability mass function gives the probability that we observe exactly \(k\) successes:
\[
P(X = k) = {n\choose k} p^k (1-p)^{n-k},
\]where \({n\choose k}\) is the number of ways to have \(k\) successes in \(n\) trials. Note that the binomial distribution assumes that the draws are independent, i.e., that \(p\) does not change between trials.
The binomial distribution naturally fits a sampling scheme, where the same experiment/observation/trial is repeated multiple times, with the same probability of success on each repetition. Classic examples include flipping a coin, computing the direction of the daily change in the stock market, or scoring a penalty in ice-hockey or football. Below, we apply the idea to studying whether a certain Premier League football club manages to avoid losing away games, that is, games played at the other team’s home stadium.

Example: Arsenal’s away game record
In the 2024/2025 Premier League season, Arsenal F.C. played 19 away games, of which they won 9, drew 8, and lost only 2. This results in 17/19 away games not lost, i.e.
\[
p = \frac{17}{19} \approx 0.895
\]
which gives us the success rate of Arsenal avoiding defeat in away games. In other words, it reflects the underlying probability that Arsenal avoids defeat in any single away match.
We assume that the away games are independent of each other, which is an assumption one could debate, as teams gain or lose momentum and face streaks of weaker or stronger opponents. However, we set aside such concerns for simplicity.
Now that we know the Arsenal’s rate of avoiding defeat in away games, we can simulate random outcomes using the binomial distributions with the R function rbinom():

rbinom(n = 10, size = 5, prob = 0.895)

 [1] 4 5 5 4 3 5 5 5 5 5


where:

n = 10: number of simulations,
size = 5: number of Bernoulli trials per simulations,
prob: probability of success per trial.

This command simulates 10 realizations of 5 away games and returns the number of successes (games not lost) in each simulation.
Other related functions:

pbinom(n, size, prob): returns the probability \(P(X\leq n)\), i.e., the probability of at most \(n\) successes.
qbinom(p, size, prob): returns the smallest integer \(k\), such that \(P(X\leq k) \geq p\), i.e., answers the question: “What is the smallest number such that at least \(p\%\) of outcomes include that number or fewer?”
dbinom(x, size, prob): returns the exact probability of observing exactly x successes, i.e., \(P(X = x) = {n \choose x} p^x (1-p)^{n-x}\).

Suppose we want to compute the probability that Arsenal avoids defeat in at least 4 out of the next 5 away games. This is:
\[
P(X \geq 4) = 1 - P(X \leq 3).
\]
Which we compute in R as:

1 - pbinom(3, size = 5, prob = 0.895)

[1] 0.9111303


Thus, it is quite likely that Arsenal will avoid defeat in 4 or 5 matches out of 5, given their high success rate in the 2024/2025 season.
How about the exact probability that Arsenal will go undefeated in the next 5 games? As we are now dealing with a discrete random variable, we get this directly from the probability mass function via dbinom:

dbinom(5, size = 5, prob = 0.895)

[1] 0.5742687


Even with a high per-game success probability, the chance of five consecutive successes is lower due to compounding!
We can use dbinom to visualize how likely different outcomes are:

x <- 0:5
probs <- dbinom(x, size = 5, prob = 0.895)

# Draw a barplot
barplot(probs, names.arg = 0:5,
        main  = "Probability distribution: Arsenal not losing in 5 away games",
        ylab  = "Probability", 
        xlab  = "Number of games without defeat",
        col   = "darkred")








Finally, with discrete random variables we can also ask: what is the minimum number of games that Arsenal avoids losing in at least 95% of simulated 10-game stretches? That is, we want the smallest \(k\) such that
\[
P(X \geq k) \geq 0.95,
\]
which is equivalently
\[
P(X \leq k-1) \leq 0.05
\]
We can compute this as

qbinom(0.05, size = 10, prob = 0.895) + 1

[1] 8


This is the smallest number \(k\) such that \(P(X \geq k) \geq 0.95\).
In sum:

rbinom: simulate n repetitions of size trials each, with success probability prob. Returns number of successes in each repetition.
pbinom: cumulative probability of at most \(k\) successes.
qbinom: quantile function, returns the minimum number of successes such that the cumulative probability is at least \(p\).
dbinom: returns exact probability of getting exactly \(x\) successes.

title: 3  Probability, simulations, and distributions
text:
4.4 Poisson distribution
As the last example of a discrete random variable, we consider the Poisson distribution. It is a fundamental distribution in probability theory and statistics when we are interested in the number of times an event happens within a fixed period of time or space. For example, it comes in handy in the following situations:

The events happen randomly (not between pre-determined intervals) and independently of each other.
The events occur at constant average rate over time, i.e. that over a several fixed-length periods, there are on average equal number of occurrences.
Two events cannot occur at exactly the same time.

The Poisson distribution is fully described by a single parameter, \(\lambda\), which is the expected number of events in the fixed time or space interval. The probability mass function of the Poisson distribution is:
\[
P(X = k) = \frac{e^{-\lambda}\lambda^k}{k!}, \quad k = 0,1,2,...,
\]
where

\(\lambda\) is the average rate of events,
\(k\) is the actual number of events observed,
\(X\) is the random variable denoting the number of events.

Examples of Poisson distributed random variables include number of customers entering a cafe, number of clicks per user on a website, the number of phone calls a salesperson makes in an hour, or the number of large earthquakes on a continent in a decade.

Example: TikTok notifications in an hour
We’ll again demonstrate the use of basic distribution functions associated with the Poisson distribution, abbreviated pois, with an example. This time, we’ll consider the number of notifications you receive from TikTok on an hourly basis. With no regard to real life, for the sake of illustration, we assume that the average hourly rate of notifications \(X\) is Poisson distributed with \(\lambda = 6\), denoted as \(X \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda = 6)\).
To simulate the number of notifications you receive in five random hours, we type:

rpois(n = 5, lambda = 6)

[1] 9 7 2 1 3


where

n: the number of observations (hours).
lambda: the expected number of notifications per hour.

As with other distributions, we again have:

ppois(k, lambda): returns the probability \(P(X\leq k)\), i.e., the probability that there are at most \(k\) occurrences of the event in a given period of time.
qpois(p, lambda): returns the smallest number \(k\), such that \(P(X\leq k) \geq p\), i.e., the smallest number such that the cumulative probability is at least \(p\).
dpois(x, lambda): returns the exact probability that there are x events, i.e. \(P(X = x)\).

For example, you might be interested in the probability of a rather quiet (notification-wise) hour, with at most 2 notifications. You get this by typing:

ppois(2, lambda = 6)

[1] 0.0619688


How depressingly unlikely! How about the probability of getting exactly \(k\) notifications in an hour? As Poisson distribution describes a discrete random variable, we get this simply by:

dpois(2, lambda = 6)

[1] 0.04461754


for two notifications. To verify, you can compute:

sum(dpois(0:2, lambda = 6))

[1] 0.0619688


Which is exactly what we got above for at most two events. As the number of events is independent, we have that
\[
P(X \leq 2) = P(X = 0) + P(X = 1) + P(X = 2).
\]
This is exactly what we got above using dpois. We can visualize the number of counts for a Poisson distribution by (you’ll learn barplot later):

x = 0:15
probs = dpois(x, lambda = 6)

barplot(probs,
        names.arg = 0:15,
        col       = "lightblue",
        border    = "black",
        main      = "Notifications from TikTok in an hour",
        xlab      = "Number of notifications",
        ylab      = "Probability")








And, as before, we can use qpois to find the number of notifications such that 90% of the time periods will have at most that many, i.e. if we observed an infinite number of hourly periods, what is the number such that 90% have no more than this number of notifications.

qpois(0.9, lambda = 6)

[1] 9


That’s a lot of notifications in an hour still! Remember, the selection \(\lambda = 6\) is not based on any real measurements. In fact, you can compute what \(\lambda\) would be for you, in case you are interested!
In summary:

rpois: simulate n hours of notifications.
ppois: cumulative probability of at most \(n\) notifications in an hour.
qpois: smallest number of notifications such that the cumulative probability is at least \(p\).
dpois: exact probability of exactly \(x\) notifications.

text:
4.5 Simulation reproducibility
Above, we introduced several probability distributions that can be used to simulate random numbers. However, computers cannot, by themselves, produce anything that is truly random. In fact, computers are just large input-output machines, designed to return exactly the same output whenever it receives the same input.
Yet earlier, we claimed that running the same command, such as rnorm(n = 5), would yield different realizations from the standard normal distribution each time it’s executed. How can this be?
To simulate randomness, computers use random number generators (RNGs), which produce sequences of numbers that appear random, even though they are fully deterministic. These are known as pseudorandom sequences, but we won’t go into how they work here. You can read more about that online (https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Random_number_generation), but the key idea is that we can control the pseudorandomness they generate. That is, if we want to, we can make R produce the same “random” sequence again and again.
This is done by setting a seed number, which guarantees that any random number generation function in R will behave deterministically. For example:

rnorm(3)

[1] -0.03787636  0.82099967  1.01533797

rnorm(3)

[1]  1.14400011 -1.36193700  0.05438636


These lines generate two different random vectors of length 3. However, if we set a seed number before drawing the numbers:

set.seed(2025)
rnorm(3)

[1] 0.6207567 0.0356414 0.7731545

set.seed(2025)
rnorm(3)

[1] 0.6207567 0.0356414 0.7731545


You’ll get exactly the same result both times!

Why use set.seed()?
You might wonder why anyone would ever want “non-random” randomness? Well, reproducibility is key in many situations:

You want to reproduce your results later, exactly as before.
You want others to be able to get the same output when they run your code.
You need to include specific simulated output in a report or an assignment.
You’re testing a function and want consistent behavior after refactoring.
You’re debugging and need consistent output to track down an issue.

In these cases, using set.seed() is advised! By setting the seed, any function that uses randomness, like rnorm, rbinom, or sample, will behave deterministically based on the seed number.
In other words: you can tell R to roll a die in exactly the same way every time. That’s something you can’t do in the real world, but is incredibly useful when doing statistics with R!
In the next Exercise, you will need another key function in R that utilizes randomness: The sample() function. In essence, it generates random samples from an object you provide, either with or without replacement. Read more about it with ?sample and answer the questions in the exercise.

5.2 if-else-statements
In statistical programming, we often need to define not only what should happen when a condition is met, but also what to do when it isn’t. This is done with the if-else-structure, where we explicitly write instructions for both outcomes of a logical condition. The structure closely resembles the typical reasoning in statistical hypothesis testing:

IF the p-value is less than 0.05 (assuming a 95% confidence level),
THEN we reject the null hypothesis.
ELSE, we fail to reject it.

In R, this kind of logic is implemented with the following syntax:

if (condition) {
  # Execute this code if condition is TRUE
} else {
  # Execute this code if condition is FALSE
}

For example, suppose you’re automating a task to assess whether the mean of a random variable is statistically different from zero. A common heuristic is to consider the ratio of the mean to its standard error: if this ratio exceeds 2, we might treat the result as statistically significant. But we also need to handle the case where it doesn’t.

ratio = 1.4 # In practice, this would be computed from data

if (abs(ratio) > 2) {
  print("The evidence suggests that the mean significantly differs from 0.")
} else {
  print("No strong evidence against a mean of zero.")
}

[1] "No strong evidence against a mean of zero."


And just like that, you’ve implemented a basic statistical decision rule. It’s easy to imagine this kind of structure being used in an automated reporting system: data comes in, a condition is evaluated, and the system communicates the results based on what was observed, perhaps to your boss or a client.
Note: the above structures are designed for scalar logic: they evaluate a single value at a time. However, in R, you can vectorize the if-else-structure with the function ifelse which takes in a vector of values for which the condition is evaluated, and let’s you specify what is returned when the condition is either TRUE or FALSE. The basic syntax is:

ifelse(condition, value_if_TRUE, value_if_FALSE)

And it works as follows:

x <- 1:5
ifelse(x >= 3, "Greater or equal to 3", "Less than 3")

[1] "Less than 3"           "Less than 3"           "Greater or equal to 3"
[4] "Greater or equal to 3" "Greater or equal to 3"


Indeed, you might have the results from, say, 10 different statistical tests stored in a vector, and you’d like to report the results. Instead of writing a for-loop, or writing a suitable lapply-code, you can simply use the vectorized ifelse function to automatically label the results based on the obtained test statistics.

text:
6.1 Why you should write your own functions
In statistical programming tasks, you’ll often find yourself performing the same computational steps repeatedly across different variables, samples, or data sets. For example, you might have to build the same statistical model across, say, country-specific samples, different decades of the same data, or different sets of variables.
One way to do these tasks is to manually repeat the modeling task in each situation by, for example, copying and pasting the code and changing the name of the data or the names of the variables. This approach is, however, inefficient, error-prone, and difficult to reproduce in the long run, especially when the number of repetitions grows. It also makes it harder to interpret and maintain large data analysis projects, both of which are important in statistical programming!
Instead, recurring programs and procedures should be encapsulated as user-defined functions. That is, given a task that is repeated multiple times in a project, it is advisable to write a function for it. This aligns with general principles of good programming practice: it reduces redundancy (less repeating) and improves modularity (programs consist of different functional units).
By defining your own functions, you gain the ability to tailor your code, and your programs, to the specific context of your analysis. For example, you may embed domain-specific decision criteria, test statistics, or reporting conventions, as all of these vary between applications.
In sum, when you delve deeper into statistical programming, you’ll likely find that writing your own functions becomes a recurring theme as it helps you:

Avoid code repetition,
Improve readability and modularity,
Tailor analyses to specific needs,
Make your work easier to test and debug.

Therefore, this section is very important for your future, so take your time to understand everything!

text:
6.2 Anatomy of a function
In R, just as in most other languages, a user-defined function consists of four core components:

Name: what you call the function. Self-explanatory, but important: should be unique and describe your function.

Technically, R allows for anonymous functions (i.e., functions without a name) that are created on the fly (e.g., in apply) but as they are not saved anywhere, they are not reusable.

Arguments: the inputs the function needs, such as data and parameters.

A function does not have to have any arguments either, for example date().

Function body: the set of instructions (code) for the function.

A function body is technically optional. but a function that does nothing is rather useless!

Return value: what the function gives back.

This is optional as well: the function does not have to return anything, but can instead print the results to the console.


The general function syntax is as follows:

my_function <- function(input){
  # Function body that defines the output
  output <- input^2 # For example, here we square the input.
  
  # Calling return() to return the output
  return(output)
}

Let’s unpack each of the components:

Name
The function name is what you (and R) will use to refer to your function later. After writing the function, the name is what you use to make it execute, so it is the first and most essential part of writing your own function.

my_function <- function(input){
  # Body: do something with input
}

Here, my_function is the name, and it can be called with different inputs like:

my_function("Stats for fun!")

NULL


However, as it does not have a body or a return value, it won’t do anything.
Good function names should have the following properties:

Descriptive: the name should reflect what your function does. If it calculates the mean, then calculate_mean() is a much better name than f1() or my_function().
Unique: if you create your own function to calculate a mean, it shouldn’t be called mean(), because that already exists. You mau still want to use the built-in mean() function, but you can’t if it’s already masked by your new function. This is called masking as it masks the other function. Also, functions and variables shouldn’t have the same name.
Consistent: when your project has multiple functions, use a consistent naming style. For example:

snake_case: a naming convention where underscores separate words, e.g., calculate_mean.
camelCase: a naming convention where capital letters separate words, e.g. calculateMean.




Arguments
The arguments of a function are the inputs it takes and operates on. They are specified within the parentheses ( ) of the function definition, with the general syntax:

my_function <- function(argument1 = value1, argument2 = value2){
  # Body: do something with arguments 1 and 2
}

Arguments can be data, parameters, or any sort of instructions required within the function body. There are several types of arguments and they work differently:

Required arguments: must be supplied every time the function is called, otherwise an error is returned.

cube <- function(x){
  # This function returns the cube of x.
  return(x^3)
}
cube()

The above function would return an error with the message:
Error in cube() : argument "x" is missing, with no default
Optional arguments with default values: these arguments are assigned a default value when the function is defined, which the user can override by supplying a new value.

power <- function(x, exponent = 2){
  # This function returns the "exponent" power of x.
  return(x^exponent)
}

power(3)

[1] 9

power(3, exponent = 3)

[1] 27


Using default arguments makes the function more flexible, as it has a “hard-coded” default behavior that can easily be changed. For example, in the above function, if you only use the power() function for squaring, you don’t have to explicitly set exponent = 2 as it is the default. This saves time when you want the function to behave the same way most of the time, but still need occasional flexibility.
No arguments: Some functions don’t require input, as they simply do something regardless of other variables. For example, the built-in function date() returns the current time and does not require any arguments:

print(paste("This material was compiled on: ", date()))

[1] "This material was compiled on:  Wed Oct 14 12:28:39 2026"



In sum, defining the arguments of a function is a key step in designing how your functions work. They follow similar best practices as functions: name them clearly (use self-explanatory names), use defaults smartly (only for arguments common to most calls), and avoid too many (too many arguments make the function hard to use).
The arguments are read by the function in the order they are defined. This means you can call the function without naming the arguments, as long as you supply the inputs in the correct order. However, if you assign arguments explicitly, the order no longer matters.
For example, with the power() function we can write:

power(2, 3)

[1] 8


to compute \(2^3\). We can also achieve this by explicitly specifying the exponent before the other argument:

power(exponent = 3, 2)

[1] 8


In other words, by default functions in R expect inputs in the correct order unless arguments are explicitly assigned to the names of the arguments. If they are, then the order does not matter.


Function body
The body of a function is what the function does: it contains the code that defines what is done for the arguments and what is ultimately returned. It is the part between the curly brackets { }, and it runs from the first to the last line every time the function is called. The body defines the behavior of your function, which can be, for example:

To make calculations: like the power() function above. These may include intermediate steps and the creation of new variables:

norm_stats <- function(data){
  # This function returns the mean and standard deviation of the data.
  x_mean = mean(data)
  x_sd   = sd(data)
  return(c("mean" = x_mean, "sd" = x_sd))
}

Data manipulation or analysis: for example, return a vector of summary statistics of a numeric vector:

summary <- function(data){
  # This function provides a statistical summary of the data.
  # It computes and returns the first and third quartiles Q1 and Q3, and the median value.
  summary = c("Q1"     = quantile(data, probs = c(0.25), names = F),
              "median" = median(data),
              "Q3"     = quantile(data, probs = c(0.75), names = F))
  return(summary)
}
summary(c(1,2,3,4,5))

    Q1 median     Q3 
     2      3      4 


Control structures: you can add flexibility or structure with if-else-statements:

set.seed(2025)
neg_or_not <- function(x){
  # This function checks if the input x is negative or non-negative.
  if( x >= 0){
    return("Non-negative")
  } else {
    return("Negative")
  }
}
neg_or_not(rnorm(1))

[1] "Non-negative"



The function body is the part that really defines the function. It gives the “recipe” or “instructions” for what is done with the inputs and then returns the result as the return value. The same best practices apply, i.e.:

Clear intermediate variable names: makes it easier to understand the function’s behavior.
Keep functions focused: a general rule of thumb is that each function should do one task, but do it well. If your function is doing many things simultaneously (this is often the case), you might consider breaking it up into different functions that do just one thing, and the original function simply calls these functions. This is often the case, and we’ll learn more about calling functions within functions in the next module!
Describe your function with comments: it’s helpful and good practice to provide comments that describe the purpose, arguments, and the return value of the function. This helps others to understand what the function does, and can even help you if you forget how your own function works later!



Detour: different styles to writing function
Previously, we introduced the conventional style to writing functions, where the curly brackets { } begin on a new line after the function definition. However, this isn’t required: functions can also be defined as one-liners, elsewhere and be anonymous. The different styles include:

One-liners:

# With curly brackets
square <- function(x) { x^2 }

# Without
square <- function(x) x ^ 2

These work identically and are valid styles for quick helper functions. However, they are generally not recommended, as the function’s structure is less clear.
Body defined elsewhere: you can also define the function body separately and evaluate it during function definition using the quote() and eval() functions:

body_sum <- quote({ x + y })
sum_xy <- function(x,y) eval(body_sum)
sum_xy(2,3)

[1] 5


This approach is very rare, and generally not recommended, though it does have niche use-cases (e.g., for dynamic functions).
Anonymous functions: as stated above, sometimes it is customary to write functions “on-the-go” as part of another function:

# This function takes the absolute value of 5 N(0,1) realizations inside sapply
sapply(rnorm(5), function(x) abs(x))

[1] 0.0356414 0.7731545 1.2724891 0.3709754 0.1628543


Conventional style: this is the most common and recommended style, and what we did earlier, where the body of the function is described between the curly brackets with each step on their own lines. Allows for commenting and improves readability.



Return value
Functions in R customarily return something. In fact, they always do (as long as the body is not empty). The return value is what the function gives back after the body is evaluated line by line. By default, R returns the last evaluated expression in the function body. However, you can also explicitly tell the function what to return using the return() function.
Let’s see how these two styles work:

Implicit return: returning the last evaluated expression. For example, the summary() function we created earlier can be streamlined as follows:

summary <- function(data){
  # This function provides a statistical summary of the data.
  # It computes and returns the first and third quartiles Q1 and Q3, and the median value.
  c("Q1"     = quantile(data, probs = c(0.25), names = F),
    "median" = median(data),
    "Q3"     = quantile(data, probs = c(0.75), names = F))
}
summary(c(1,2,3,4,5))

    Q1 median     Q3 
     2      3      4 


Here, the summary vector is no longer assigned to an intermediate variable. Instead, it is returned implicitly by placing it on the last line. Note that if the last line was an assignment, e.g., summary = c("Q1" =... the summary vector is returned invisibly, i.e. that if you call summary(c(1,2,3,4,5)), you’d see nothing, but if you assigned it to a variable, it would hold the summary vector.
Explicit return: using the return() function. Often, it is helpful to be explicit about what is being returned. We saw this earlier in the first draft of the summary() function. return() is especially useful when:

Returning multiple values:

summary <- function(data){
  # This function provides a statistical summary of the data.
  # It computes and returns the first and third quartiles Q1 and Q3, and the median value.
  Q1  = quantile(data, probs = c(0.25), names = F)
  med = median(data)
  Q3  = quantile(data, probs = c(0.75), names = F)
  return(c("Q1" = Q1, "median" = med, "Q3" = Q3))
}
summary(c(1,2,3,4,5))

    Q1 median     Q3 
     2      3      4 


Using conditional logic: as above with the neg_or_not() function:

neg_or_not <- function(x){
  # This function check if the input x is negative or non-negative.
  if( x >= 0){
    return("Non-negative")
  } else {
    return("Negative")
  }
}

Here, the return value depends on the input. If x >= 0 is TRUE, the function returns the character string "Non-negative", otherwise it returns "Negative". This is known as conditional early exit.


The return value is what completes the function. It defines what the function gives back when called with specific arguments. It can be either implicit or explicit, depending on your needs:

Use explicit returns when:

Your function has conditional logic (such as early exist).
You want to make the return value clear and obvious.
You’re debugging and want control over what is returned.

Use implicit returns when:

You’re writing tiny helper functions or clear one-liners.
The return values is self-evident from the last line.


Whichever style you choose, be consistent throughout. Also, remember to describe the return value in your function comments, as this helps both other users and your future self in understanding how the function behaves.


Detour: Printing inside a function
Up to this point, the things that happen in the body of the function were unknown to the user of the function. Sometimes it is useful to print intermediate results to the console, so that the user knows what is happening. For example, if the function simulates large quantities of random variables, and is therefore slow, or if we want to understand what happens at different parts for debugging, it might be useful to be able to communicate messages from inside the function. In R, the most common ways to do this are:

print(): sends the output to the console in a readable format.
cat(): concatenates and outputs text and/or variables. Typically used for user-friendly messages.
message(), warning(), and stop(): used for special cases like error handling, which we’ll cover in the next Module.

Let’s next see how print() and cat() work in practice:

print(): used to print an R object (like a vector or data frame) clearly:

summary <- function(data){
  print(data)
  # This function provides a statistical summary of the data.
  # It computes and returns the first and third quartiles Q1 and Q3, and the median value.
  Q1  = quantile(data, probs = c(0.25), names = F)
  med = median(data)
  Q3  = quantile(data, probs = c(0.75), names = F)
  return(c("Q1" = Q1, "median" = med, "Q3" = Q3))
}
summary(c(1,2,3,4,5))

[1] 1 2 3 4 5


    Q1 median     Q3 
     2      3      4 


Here, the input vector is printed before anything is done. In your RStudio session, this print would appear in the Console.
cat(): typically used to create clean, readable messages, that combine text and variable values. You can also decide how lines are separated via the sep = "\n" argument:

cat_demonst <- function(iterations = 5){
  print("New line at each iteration")
  for(i in 1:iterations){
    cat("Iteration: ", i, sep = "\n")
  }
  print("Same line at each iteration")
  for(i in 1:iterations){
    cat("Iteration: ", i, " ")
  }
}
cat_demonst()

[1] "New line at each iteration"
Iteration: 
1
Iteration: 
2
Iteration: 
3
Iteration: 
4
Iteration: 
5
[1] "Same line at each iteration"
Iteration:  1  Iteration:  2  Iteration:  3  Iteration:  4  Iteration:  5  


The sep = "\n" in cat() means “new line”.

In sum, printing messages to the console is useful when:

Debugging: when something’s wrong inside your function, you can use printing to trace where the problem is.
Informing the user: sometimes you might want to report what is currently done inside the function.
Exploring: printing is particularly useful when developing functions, as you can ensure that the data objects are of the correct structure before writing the next line in the function.

text:
6.3 Example: writing a function to center data
In the previous Module, we learned about the built-in function scale(), which can be used to mean-center data. For learning purposes, we’ll now write our own mean-centering function from scratch. This gives us a chance to review the key components of functions. We’ll also highlight a few best practices for writing clean and user-friendly functions.

Step 1: Initializing a function
We begin by creating an empty function with the function() keyword. It’s important to choose a clear and descriptive name so others (and your future self) can see what the function does from its name:

center_func <- function() {
  
}

And there, we have the outline of the function: a function called center_func(). Currently, it does not take any input or perform any actions, but is still already a function, and it returns NULL.


Step 2: Function arguments and body
To make the function do what we are after, we want it to take a numeric vector as input and return that vector with its mean subtracted. The formula is:
\[
\tilde{x}_i =  x_i - \bar{x}
\]
where \(\bar{x}\) is the average value \(\bar{x} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_n x_i\). This brings the mean of the vector to zero and therefore the new centered variable can be thought of as absolute deviations from the mean. We therefore add an input argument x, and update the function body to compute and return the centered vector:

center_func <- function(x){
  # This function centers the input data vector x.
  # First we compute the mean, using the length and sum of the vector.
  n       <- length(x)
  x_sum   <- sum(x)
  x_mean  <- (1/n)*x_sum
  
  # Then the centered vector x_tilde
  x_tilde <- x - x_mean
  
  # Finally return the centered variable.
  return(x_tilde)
}

Where we first compute the mean/average by hand, and then subtract it from each element in x. Note that we could simply use mean() to compute the mean as well. We can now try the function:

center_func(c(1,2,3))

[1] -1  0  1


And by hand, we get that \(\bar{x} = \frac{1 + 2+ 3}{3} = 2\), and therefore the expected output is \((1 - 2, 2 - 2, 3 - 2) = (-1,0,1)\), so the function appears to be working!


Step 3: Default arguments
To add more flexibility, we now want the function to return the original data if the user explicitly asks for it. For the present example, this option is counter-intuitive but is implemented for learning purposes to understand how default arguments work in practice. Therefore, we add a logical argument that allows for specifying whether centering should be done:

center_func <- function(x, center = TRUE){
  # This function centers the input data vector x.
  
  # First check if centering is actually required
  if (!center){ 
    cat("No centering this time.")
    return(x) 
  }
  # First we compute the mean, using the length and sum of the vector.
  n       <- length(x)
  x_sum   <- sum(x)
  x_mean  <- (1/n)*x_sum
  
  # Then the centered vector x_tilde
  x_tilde <- x - x_mean
  
  # Finally return the centered variable.
  return(x_tilde)
}

Now:

center_func(x) returns the centered data (default behavior).
center_func(x, center = FALSE): returns the original data and prints out a message informing the user that no centering was done.

The argument center = TRUE is an example of a default argument that is aligned with the expected or standard behavior of the function, which can be altered if the user so desires.
This example was somewhat arbitrary, as mean-centering is easily achieved with scale(x, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE), and we computed the mean by hand instead of mean(). These functions also offer further arguments that can be readily used to add more flexibility with ease. For example, we can handle missing values in mean() with the argument na.rm, and add this as an optional argument in our own function. We’ll cover more advanced topics like this in the next module, where we continue with the User-defined functions - Part II.

text:
7.1 Everything starts with plot()
The plot() function is the most fundamental way to create graphs in R. It can be used for scatter plots (points scattered on a two-dimensional plane), line plots (the points connected by lines), and many other types of plots. Knowing its core arguments helps us understand how to create plots effectively. The general syntax is:

plot(x, y, type, col, lwd, lty, pch, xlab, ylab, main, xlim, ylim, pty)

where

x, y: the data to be plotted. Typically, x` is the variable for the horizontal (x-axis) and y is for the vertical (y-axis). You can also provide only y, and plot() will automatically use the index as x.
type: Controls the type of the plot:

"p": default, points.
"l": lines.
"b": both points and lines.
"h": histogram-like vertical lines.
"n": no plotting, useful for setting up the plot area before adding points or lines manually.

col: color of the plotted points or lines. Can be a color name such as "red" or "blue" (for more color names, type colors() or search the internet), or a number. You can also pass a vector of colors to assign one per observations.
lwd, lty: line width (thickness) and line type (either by number or name). Default width is 1, and increasing it will make thicker lines. Different line types are:

0: blank (no line)
1: solid (default)
2: dashed
3: dotted
4: dotdash
5: longdash
6: twodash

pch: plotting character or symbol for points. Common values are:

0: square
1: open circle (default)
2: triangle
3: plus
4: cross
19: solid circle (filled)
You can check all point styles here. For point symbols with pch from 21 to 25, you can define a fill colour with the additional parameter bg.

xlab, ylab: labels for the x-axis and y-axis.
main: Title of the plot.
xlim, ylim: limits for the x-axis and y-axis (vectors of length 2).
pty: plotting region shape:

"s": square plot region (equal width and height).
"m": default, rectangular plot region.


Let’s see how these work with a few examples. First, the very basic and simple scatter plot:

set.seed(2025)
x <- 1:100
y <- x + rnorm(100, sd = 10)
plot(x,y)








Here, we have a simple linear y = x, but the observationss are disturbed by normally distributed error (a common thing in statistical modeling as you’ll learn in Module 5!). Let’s make it with a thick blue line instead of points:

plot(x,y, type = "l", col = "blue", lwd = 2)








Maybe, both points and lines instead:

plot(x,y, type = "b", col = "blue", lwd = 2)








Adjust the line and point types and change colour:

plot(x,y, type = "b", col = "olivedrab3", lwd = 1, pch = 19, lty = 2)








Let’s add some titles to describe the plot and change the colour and line and point types once again:

plot(x,y, type = "b", col = "maroon", lwd = 1, pch = 22, bg = "steelblue1", lty = 4,
     xlab = "X values", ylab = "Y values", main = "Example plot of a linear relationship")








And just like that, we now know how to plot basically anything in R, so let’s next plot something we are interested in!

text:
7.2 Plotting Normal PDFs with curve()
Earlier, we learned that the PDF of the Normal distribution is:
\[
f(x;\mu, \sigma) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi \sigma^2}} \exp \left( -\frac{(x - \mu)^2}{2\sigma^2} \right),
\]
and it is known as the bell curve due to its shape, which is defined by two parameters:

Mean \(\mu\): the center of the distribution. Controls the location of the distribution.
Standard deviation \(\sigma\): controls how spread out the distribution is.

In R, we can use the dnorm() function to compute the values of the density function for a given \(x\), mean \(\mu\), and standard deviation \(\sigma\). We can demonstrate the effects of these parameters by defining a range of values for them, and then plotting the corresponding distributions. To do this, we use the curve() function, which allows you to plot a univariate function over a certain range and it has the following basic syntax:

curve(expr, from = NULL, to = NULL, add = FALSE)

where

expr: the name of a function, or an expression written as a function of x (e.g. x^2).
from: the starting value of the interval for x.
to: the ending value of the interval for x.
add: a logical: if TRUE, then the curve is added to an existing plot, if NA, starts a new plot and takes defaults from the previous plot. Taken as FALSE if there is no existing plot.

The function we want to plot is dnorm, and since we have a range of values for the Normal distribution, we will first create an empty plot and then add to it in a for-loop:

set.seed(2025 + 3) # +3 is because nice colours were searched...

# Initialize an empty plotting area
plot(NULL, xlim = c(-5, 10), ylim = c(0, 0.8),
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Density", main = "Normal PDFs with Different Parameters")

# Parameters for normal distribution
means = -3:3
sds   = seq(0.5, 2, length = 7)
cols  = sample(colors(), 7)

# Add each pdf to the plot in a for-loop
for (i in 1:length(means)) {
  curve(dnorm(x, mean = means[i], sd = sds[i]), from = -5, to = 10, col = cols[i], lwd = 2, lty = i, add = TRUE)
}

# Add a legend that describes what the plot shows
legend("topright", legend = paste0("N(", means, ",", round(sds,1), ")"),
       col = cols, lwd = 2, lty = 1:7)








where we have also used the plotting function legend() which has the following arguments:

x, y: the x and y co-ordinates to position the legend. Alternatively, as we did, you can use keywords such as "topright", "bottomleft", etc.
legend: what the legend says, i.e. a character string (or an expression).
lty, lwd, pch, cols: the arguments used to create what is shown in the plot (here, curves).
You can do a lot more with legends, see ?legend for more infromation.

section: 7.3 Plotting random samples with histogram() and rug()
text:
7.3 Plotting random samples with histogram() and rug()
Next, we’ll pick one normal distribution and generate a random sample from it, and compare the sample mean to the theoretical mean via graphical tools. First, generate a sample of 100 observations from \(N(3, 2)\):

set.seed(2025 + 1) 
# Set parameters
n     <- 100
mu    <- 3
sigma <- 2

# Generate random sample
r_sample <- rnorm(n, mu, sigma) # Note that rnorm expects arguments in this order, so this is equal to rnorm(n, mean = mu, sd = sigma)
mean(r_sample)

[1] 2.803908


A common way to visualize a random sample of continuous random variables is by using a histogram with the hist function. A histogram groups the data into bins (intervals) and shows how many observations fall into each bin using vertical bars. It has the following general syntax:

hist(x, breaks = "Sturges", probability = FALSE...)

where

x: the numeric vector of values to be binned into the histogram.
breaks: controls how the data range is split into bins. It can be:

A single number, e.g. breaks = 30, to set the number of bins,
a vector of break points
or a string like "Sturges" (default), "Scott", or "FD" for automatic rules (see ?hist for more).

probability: a logical; if TRUE, the histogram is scaled to show probability densities (bins scaled by total number of observations), if FALSE, shows raw counts.
...: includes, for example, col, xlab, ylab, and other graphical parameters passed to the underlying plot() function.

With our random sample, we get:

hist(r_sample, xlab = "X values", main = "Histogram of Sampled Normal Data")








To contrast this with how the PDF looks like, we can overlay it on the histogram by:

hist(r_sample, probability = TRUE, col = "darkseagreen", 
     xlab = "X values", ylab = "Density", 
     main = "Histogram of Sampled Normal Data")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma), col = "tomato2", lwd = 3, add = TRUE)








Another way to plot the sample is via rug(), which has the general syntax:

rug(x, side = 1, ticksize = 0.03)

where

x: the numeric vector of values to be shown.
side: the axis to draw the ticks on (defaults to 1).
ticksize: length of the tick marks as a fraction of the plot region.

It works like this:

# Plot PDF again
curve(dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma), from = mu - 4*sigma, to = mu + 4*sigma,
      col = "red", lwd = 2, ylab = "Density", xlab = "x",
      main = "Normal PDF and Sample Summary")
# Add rug plot of sample values on x-axis
rug(r_sample, ticksize = 0.1)








It adds a “rug” that shows where the realizations land on the x-axis.

title: 3  Probability, simulations, and distributions
text:
7.4 Adding lines with abline()
One of the most fundamental ideas in statistical inference is that a sample statistic can be used as an approximation of a population parameter. For example, the sample mean \(\bar{x}\) is commonly used to estimate the population mean \(\mu\) when the data is normally distributed (it is an unbiased estimate of the population mean, something we’ll cover in the next Module). We can use simulation to make this idea intuitive by visualizing how a sample behaves in relation to the distribution it was drawn from. To do this, we use the abline() function, as it allows us to draw straight lines into the plot, so we can draw two vertical lines: one for the sample mean (the estimate) and one for the population mean (the ground truth). The general syntax is:

abline(a = NULL, b = NULL, h = NULL, v = NULL, ...)

where

a: intercept of a straight line (used with b for y = a + bx).
b: Slope of a straight line (used with a).
h: draws a horizontal line at y = h.
v: draws a vertical line at x = v.
...: other graphical parameters passed to the underlying plot() function

So, for our example with the histogram, we can simply add the two means by:

hist(r_sample, probability = TRUE, col = "darkseagreen", 
     xlab = "X values", ylab = "Density", 
     main = "Histogram of Sampled Normal Data")
curve(dnorm(x, mean = mu, sd = sigma), col = "tomato2", lwd = 3, add = TRUE)
abline(v = mean(r_sample), col = "lightskyblue1", lwd = 2) # The sample mean
abline(v = 3, col = "midnightblue", lwd = 2) # The population mean








They are pretty close! In the next Module, we’ll get deeper into the basics of statistical inference in R, and we’ll compute some confidence intervals on the sample mean derived here and get familiar with how we can verify theoretical results by simulation studies. For example, we’ll learn how to simulate the idea underlying many theoretical statistical results: that of repeated sampling!

text:
7.5 Setting graphical parameters with par()
As the final thing in this module, we’ll briefly go through the basic global graphical parameters that can be set or queried with the function par(). The most common graphical parameters that you can change are:

mfcol, mfrow: a vector of the form c(nr, nc). After setting this parameter, all subsequent figures will be plotted in an nr-by-nc array either by columns (mfcol) or by rows (mfrow), respectively. This means that, for example, if you set mfrow(1, 3), the subsequent figures will be plotted in an array with one row and three columns (see below for an example).
mar, mai: sets the margins of the four sides of the plot in lines of text (mar) or in inches (mai). Should be a numerical vector of the form c(bottom, left, top, right).
oma, omi: sets the outer margins in lines of text (oma) or in inches (omi). Should be a numerical vector of the form c(bottom, left, top, right).

For example, we can plot three histograms side by side by as follows:

r_sample1 <- rnorm(100, mean = 0, sd = 1)
r_sample2 <- rnorm(100, mean = 3, sd = 2)
r_sample2 <- rnorm(100, mean = 6, sd = 0.5)

# Set the graphical parameter to fill the plot row-wise with one row and three columns
par(mfrow = c(1,3))

# Plot the three histograms
hist(r_sample1, probability = TRUE, col = "darkseagreen", 
     xlab = "X values", ylab = "Density", 
     main = "Histogram 1")
hist(r_sample1, probability = TRUE, col = "salmon4", 
     xlab = "X values", ylab = "Density", 
     main = "Histogram 2")
hist(r_sample1, probability = TRUE, col = "steelblue3", 
     xlab = "X values", ylab = "Density", 
     main = "Histogram 3")

text:
5 Descriptive statistics
In this Module, we take the first steps from descriptive statistics to formal statistical inference, using the tools R has to offer. While we can summarize and understand the observed data through descriptive statistics, statistical inference is about going beyond that: we aim to make inferences about population-level distributional characteristics. The term “population” refers to the underlying stochastic process that generated the data, which is of interest to us as statisticians.
We’ll begin by reviewing key summary statistics that describe the data: its location, spread, and shape, as well as graphical tools we have at our disposal for visualizing these key aspects of the data.
From there, we’ll move toward the key inferential question:
To answer this, we’ll look into the concepts of sampling distributions, confidence intervals, and hypothesis testing. We focus on computational tools in R that help us understand and verify different theoretical results based on the idea of repeated sampling. This builds intuition and enhances your coding skills to approach more complex subjects in later studies.
This module focuses on three key ideas:
crumbs: 4  Basic statistical inference

title: 4  Basic statistical inference
text:
5.1 Measures of central tendency
When describing data, as measures of some real phenomenon, one of the most natural questions to ask is: what is a typical observation? That is, around which value do the realizations tend to fall? It may very well be that there are several “typical” values, but here we will only focus on unimodal distributions, i.e., data where the observations are centered around one point.
There isn’t just one way to define the “center” of the distribution: depending on other characteristics, the different measures might vary significantly. However, in R and in statistics, the most common measures include:

Mean (average): the arithmetic average of the values. This measure is probably the most widely used both in and outside of statistics, and therefore perhaps the most misunderstood. Arithmetic average is computed as the sum of the observations divided by their count, which makes it mathematically convenient but also sensitive to extreme values (outliers).
Median: the middle value of the data after ordering it. In contrast to mean, the median is robust to outliers and skewed data as we will soon see. For asymmetric data, the median is sometimes considered a better measure of central tendency than the mean.
Mode: the most frequent value in the data. Useful with categorical data, where the set of outcomes is a discrete random variable.

To use these in R, we have:

mean(x, trim = 0, na.rm = FALSE)
median(x, na.rm = FALSE)

where:

x: a numeric vector containing the values whose mean is to be computed.
trim: the fraction (between 0 and 0.5) of observations to be trimmed from each end before computing the mean. Useful for ignoring extreme outliers when computing the mean.
na.rm: logical to tell if missing values should be removed. TRUE ignores NAs, FALSE returns NA if any are present.

There is no built-in function to compute the mode, but you can get it easily by:

set.seed(2025)
# Generate a random sample of discrete random variable.
discrete_rv <- sample(LETTERS[1:4], 20, replace = TRUE)

# Tabulate the counts of each category
table(discrete_rv)

discrete_rv
A B C D 
5 3 8 4 

# Choose the category with the most occurrences
names(which.max(table(discrete_rv)))

[1] "C"


We’ll demonstrate how mean and median behave with samples drawn from continuous distributions that are either symmetric or asymmetric.

Example 1: Symmetric distribution
In a symmetric distribution, the mean and the median coincide. The Normal distribution, for example, is symmetric, so we can use it to demonstrate this. With visualization tools from Module 3, we get:

set.seed(2025)

# Generate a sample of 1000 observations from N(15, 7)
symm_sample <- rnorm(n = 1000, mean = 15, sd = 7)

# Plot the histogram
hist(symm_sample, breaks = 40, col = "powderblue", probability = TRUE, 
     main = "Symmetric distribution: N(15, 7)",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Density")
# Plot the PDF
curve(dnorm(x, mean = 15, sd = 7), add = TRUE, col = "royalblue4", lwd = 2)
# Plot a vertical line at the mean of the sample
abline(v = mean(symm_sample), col = "lightgoldenrod3", lwd = 3, lty = 2)
abline(v = median(symm_sample), col = "indianred1", lwd = 3, lty = 3)
legend("topright", legend = c("Mean", "Median"), 
       col = c("lightgoldenrod3", "indianred1"), lty = c(2,3), lwd = 3)








And we see that the mean and the median lie on top of each other! This reflects the symmetry of the normal distribution: the middle value is often very close to the mean, especially with large samples. However, things change when there are larger deviations on one side of the distribution:


Example 2: Asymmetric distribution
To demonstrate how mean and median change with asymmetric distributions, we now introduce the exponential distribution. We will not go into its details, but merely note that it is positively skewed (long right tail), which pulls the mean (average) toward the right tail:

set.seed(2025)

# Generate a sample of 1000 observations from N(15, 7)
asymm_sample <- rexp(n = 1000, rate = 1)

mean(asymm_sample) > median(asymm_sample)

[1] TRUE

# Plot the histogram
hist(asymm_sample, breaks = 40, col = "powderblue", probability = TRUE, 
     main = "Asymmetric distribution: Exponential(1)",
     xlab = "x", ylab = "Density")
# Plot the PDF
curve(dexp(x, rate = 1), add = TRUE, col = "royalblue4", lwd = 2)
# Plot a vertical line at the mean of the sample
abline(v = mean(asymm_sample), col = "lightgoldenrod3", lwd = 3, lty = 2)
abline(v = median(asymm_sample), col = "indianred1", lwd = 3, lty = 3)
legend("topright", legend = c("Mean", "Median"), 
       col = c("lightgoldenrod3", "indianred1"), lty = c(2,3), lwd = 3)








We see that there is a clear gap between the mean and the median, indicating the fact that the mean is dragged to the right by the few very large observations. The median, however, is robust to these: it remains at the 50th percentile, which is located further to the left due to many observations being close to zero.


Summary
While the question of which descriptive statistic best expresses central tendencies is always domain-specific and depends highly on the research question, a few rough lines can be drawn:

If the data is approximately symmetric and free of outliers, use and report the mean. It is mathematically convenient and connects naturally to estimates of population parameters for the normal distribution.
If the data is skewed or has extreme outliers, use and report the median.

Neither of these measures can describe a data set well on a stand-alone basis, and it is not advised to use them alone. They should be accompanied by other descriptive statistics that together provide a better summary of the data. We’ll turn to these next.
