8.1 Linear regression analysis with one explanatory variable
Linear regression analysis focuses on understanding and modeling the linear relationship between two observed variables. In all regression models, we have two types of variables:

Dependent variable: the variable whose variability we try to explain (also known as response variable, measured variable, explained variable, outcome variable).
Independent variables: the variables used to explain the variability in the dependent variable (also known as explanatory variables, predictors, regressor, covariate).

In other words, we try to explain the portion of the dependent variable’s variability that can be attributed to variability in the independent variable(s).
In this section, we’ll cover linear regression models with only one independent variable. Let \(y_1, y_2, \dots, y_n\) denote the observed variables of the dependent variable \(Y_i\) at observations \(i=1,\dots,n\), and \(x_1, x_2, \dots, x_n\) denote the observed values of the independent variable. We assume that the independent variable values \(x_i\) are fixed and not random.
Next, assume that there exists a statistical linear relationship between the observed values \(y_i\) and \(x_i\), which can be expressed as:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_i + \varepsilon_i, \quad i = 1,\dots,n.\]
This equation defines the simple linear regression (one independent variable), in which:

\(y_i\) is the observed value of the random variable \(Y\).
\(x_i\) is the observed value of the independent variable (treated as non-random/fixed).
\(\varepsilon_i\) is the random and unobserved error term.

The model has the following regression coefficients:

\(\beta_0\): the intercept (a non-random and unknown constant).
\(\beta_1\): the slope / regression coefficient corresponding to the independent variable \(x\) (a non-random and unknown constant).

These coefficients are parameters to be estimated from the data, and are assumed to be constant across all observations. The error term \(\varepsilon_i\) usually has the following standard assumptions:

\(\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_i] = 0, \,\, i = 1,2,\dots,n\). The error terms are on average equal to zero, that is, the observations are distributed around the estimated regression line.
\(\text{Var}(\varepsilon_i) = \sigma^2, \,\, i = 1, \dots,n\). The error terms are homoskedastic, that is, they have equal variances across observations.
\(\text{Cov}(\varepsilon_i, \varepsilon_j) = 0, \,\, i \neq j\). The error terms are uncorrelated.
In addition, sometimes the error terms are assumed to be normally distributed: \(\varepsilon_i \sim \mathrm{N}(0,\sigma^2), \,\, i = 1,2,\dots,n\). Note that this assumption includes assumption 1 and 2.

We’ll omit estimation derivations (covered in other courses) and instead focus on the R tools to fit and evaluate linear models.

Fitting our first model with lm()
The function for fitting linear regression models (i.e., estimating the coefficients) in R is lm(). It has the following general syntax:

lm(formula, data, subset, weights, na.action)

where:

formula: a symbolic description of the model to be fitted. A typical model has the form response ~ terms, where “response” refers to the response variable, i.e. the dependent variable \(Y\), and “terms” refer to the names of the independent variables.
data: optional, includes the (named) variables that appear in the model formula. If the variables are not found in data, R looks for them in the environment from which lm() is called.
subset: an optional vector specifying a subset of observations to be used in the fitting process. Omitted here.
na.action: specifies what should happen when the data contains missing values (NAs). The default and recommended option is na.omit, other options are omitted here.

These are only the most important arguments, and you can learn the rest by typing ?lm.
To demonstrate the use of lm(), we will consider the built-in data set airquality. It consists of 153 daily air quality measurements for the following six variables in New York (May to September 1973):

Ozone: mean ozone in part per billion from 1300 to 1500 hours at Roosevelt Island.
Solar.R: solar radiation in Langleys in the frequency band 4000-7700 Angstroms from 0800 to 1200 hours at Central Park.
Wind: average wind speed in miles per hour at 0700 and 1000 hours at LaGuardia Airport.
Temp: maximum daily temperature in degrees Fahrenheit at LaGuardia Airport.
Month: month number.
Day: day number.

We will first model the relationship between ozone levels and solar radiation:

model1 <- lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R, data = airquality, na.action = "na.omit")

Now the output of the function is stored in the variable model1. lm() returns an object of class "lm", which is a named list containing at least the following components:

coefficients: a named vector of the estimated regression coefficients \(\widehat{\beta}_j\) for \(j = 0,1\) in our simple example here.
fitted.values: the fitted mean values \(\widehat{y}_i = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 x_i\).
residuals: the residuals, which correspond to the values of the dependent variable minus the fitted values: \(\widehat{\varepsilon}_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\). Note that residuals are the empirical counterpart of the error terms \(\varepsilon\) that are never observed, that is, they are estimates.
Other components, such as rank, df.residual, call, and terms, which you can explore further with ?lm.

These provide the estimates for the regression coefficients, as well as the corresponding fitted values and residuals, which are of primary importance in linear models. For example:

model1$coefficients

(Intercept)     Solar.R 
 18.5987278   0.1271653 


The values above correspond to \(\beta_0\) and \(\beta_1\) in the linear model equation, such that:
\[\widehat{y}_i = 18.60 + 0.13\cdot x_i \quad \mathrm{and} \quad \widehat{\varepsilon}_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i, \quad i = 1,\dots,n.\]
Here, \(\widehat{y}_i\) and \(\widehat{\varepsilon}_i\) are the fitted values and the residuals, respectively, as specified above.


Accessing model components
There are two main ways to access the components of an lm object: directly using the $ operator on the model object, or by using wrapper functions designed for lm objects.

Using the $ operator
The lm object returned by the lm() function is essentially a named list containing several components. You can extract these components by using the $ operator followed by the component name.
For example, to access the estimated regression coefficients, fitted values and residuals, you can use:

model1$coefficients        # Extracts the regression coefficient (intercept and slope, beta_0 and beta_1)

(Intercept)     Solar.R 
 18.5987278   0.1271653 

head(model1$fitted.values) # Extracts the fitted values from the model

       1        2        3        4        7        8 
42.76013 33.60423 37.54635 58.40146 56.62114 31.18809 

head(model1$residuals)     # Extracts the residuals

         1          2          3          4          7          8 
 -1.760129   2.395770 -25.546353 -40.401458 -33.621144 -12.188090 


This gives direct access to the underlying numeric vectors or matrices stored within the model object.


Using wrapper functions
R provides convenient wrapper functions that extract commonly used components from lm objects. These functions not only make the code cleaner but sometimes also perform additional checks or computations.
Two of the most frequently used wrapper functions are:

coefficients() or its shorthand coef(): returns the vector of estimated regression coefficients.

coefficients(model1)

(Intercept)     Solar.R 
 18.5987278   0.1271653 

# or equivalently
coef(model1)

(Intercept)     Solar.R 
 18.5987278   0.1271653 


fitted(): returns the fitted values \(\widehat{y}\).
residuals(): returns the residuals \(\widehat{\varepsilon}_i = y_i - \widehat{y}_i\).

These wrapper functions make your code more readable and are the preferred way to access these components.
However, we often want to conduct statistical inference on these estimates. In such cases, statistics based on the sampling distribution of the coefficients, such as confidence intervals and t-test statistics for the null hypothesis \(\beta_j = 0\), are of interest. These are not directly returned by the lm() function call, but luckily there are wrappers built for lm objects that compute these for us, and we’ll turn to these next.



Using summary() to interpret coefficients and significance
The summary() function produces detailed summaries of model objects returned by lm() (and other modeling functions). While the internal workings of summary() are beyond the the scope of this course, it is important to understand the main components it returns when applied to an lm object. For example:

model1_summary <- summary(model1)

Here model1_summary is a named list that includes key elements such as:

coefficients: the estimated regression coefficients with their standard errors, t-statistics testing the null hypothesis \(\beta_j = 0\), and the associated p-values. This helps you assess the significance and direction of each independent variable’s effect.
residuals: the residuals, which are the differences between observed and predicted values, also stored in the original lm object.
sigma: the residual standard error, \(\widehat{\sigma} = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n-p} \sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{y}_i)^2 }\), where \(n\) is the number of observations, \(p\) is the number of parameters estimated (including the intercept), \(y_i\) are observed values, and \(\widehat{y}_i\) are fitted values.

Understanding these components will help you interpret your linear model’s fit and the significance of its predictors. They form the backbone of the inferential tools the linear regression model offers, and are hence at the very heart of statistical modeling and inference.
For example:

# View the coefficients table (estimates, standard errors, t-values, p-values)
print(model1_summary$coefficients)

              Estimate Std. Error  t value     Pr(>|t|)
(Intercept) 18.5987278 6.74790416 2.756223 0.0068560215
Solar.R      0.1271653 0.03277629 3.879795 0.0001793109

# Access the residual standard error
cat("Residual standard error:", model1_summary$sigma, "\n")

Residual standard error: 31.33457 


Below, we introduce the columns of this table. A more comprehensive summary is obtained by printing the whole model1_summary object:

model1_summary


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ Solar.R, data = airquality, na.action = "na.omit")

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-48.292 -21.361  -8.864  16.373 119.136 

Coefficients:
            Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) 18.59873    6.74790   2.756 0.006856 ** 
Solar.R      0.12717    0.03278   3.880 0.000179 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 31.33 on 109 degrees of freedom
  (42 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.1213,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.1133 
F-statistic: 15.05 on 1 and 109 DF,  p-value: 0.0001793


where:

Residuals: gives a summary of the distribution of the residuals.
Coefficients: prints a table with the following columns:

Estimate: the estimated regression coefficient.
Std. Error: the standard error of the regression coefficient’s sampling distribution (not introduced in this course).
t value: the t-test statistic corresponding to testing the null hypothesis \(\beta_j = 0\).

Note: the details of this test are omitted here, as they are introduced in other courses, but the test statistic is \(t = \frac{|\widehat{\beta}|}{\text{se}(\widehat{\beta})} \sim t_{n-p-1}\), where \(\text{se}(\widehat{\beta})\) is the standard error of the coefficient and is printed in the model summary.

Pr(>|t|): the p-value associated with the above t-test.

In addition, we get the residual standard error and the associated degrees of freedom.

We will skip the interpretation of the results from the model summary above for now. We will briefly discuss how to interpret such results when we introduce multiple linear regression below.


Visualizing the regression line on a scatterplot
As discussed before, we can add the regression line to a scatterplot using the function abline(). Below is an example that plots the original data and adds the fitted regression line:

# First remove NAs
airquality2 <- na.omit(airquality)
# Scatterplot of Ozone vs Solar.R
plot(airquality2$Solar.R, airquality2$Ozone,
     main = "Ozone vs Solar Radiation",
     xlab = "Solar Radiation (Langleys)",
     ylab = "Ozone (ppb)",
     pch = 19, col = "lightskyblue2")

# Add the regression line from the linear model
abline(model1, col = "plum4", lwd = 2)








This plot shows the data points with light blue dots and overlays the estimated regression line in purple. The line visually summarizes the linear relationship between solar radiation and ozone levels, and we see that the relationship is positive: the higher the solar radiation, the higher the mean ozone level, on average. However, the assumption of constant variance might be violated, can you tell why?

text:
8.2 Linear regression with multiple independent variables
So far, we have looked at modeling the relationship between a dependent variable and a single independent variable. In many real-world settings, however, the outcome of interest may vary with several factors at the same time. Linear regression extends naturally to include multiple explanatory variables, allowing us to model and quantify their combined influence on the dependent variable.
Suppose we have a dependent variable \(Y_i\) measured for \(n\) observations, \(i=1,\dots,n\), and \(p\) independent variables \(x_{i1}, x_{i2}, \dots, x_{ip}\). The multiple linear regression model can be written as:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x_{i1} + \beta_2 x_{i2} + \cdots + \beta_p x_{ip} + \varepsilon_i, \quad i = 1,\dots,n.\]
Here:

\(Y_i\) is the dependent variable.
\(x_{ij}\) is the observed value of the \(j\)-th independent variable for observation \(i\).
\(\varepsilon_i\) is the error term, representing variation in \(Y_i\) not explained by the independent variables.
\(\beta_0, \beta_1, \dots, \beta_p\) are the regression coefficients to be estimated.

The interpretation of the coefficients is analogous to the simple regression case:

\(\beta_0\) is the intercept, representing the expected value of \(Y\) when all \(x_{ij} = 0\).
\(\beta_j\) (for \(j = 1,\dots,p\)) is the expected change in \(Y\) for a one-unit increase in \(x_{ij}\), holding all other independent variables constant.

As before, the error terms are assumed to satisfy the standard regression assumptions.
This framework lets us model more complex relationships where multiple variables jointly affect the outcome. It also allows us to control for confounding effects and identify the unique contribution of each predictor.
Next, we’ll see how to fit such models in R using the lm() function with multiple independent variables, and how to interpret the output.

Extending lm() to handle several predictors
In R, fitting a multiple linear regression model works much like the simple case. The difference is simply that we include additional independent variables in the formula.
Continuing with our airquality example, suppose we want to explain the variation in mean ozone levels using both the solar radiation (Solar.R) and the temperature (Temp). We can fit a multiple the model as follows:

model2 <- lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Temp, data = airquality)
summary(model2)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ Solar.R + Temp, data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-36.610 -15.976  -2.928  12.371 115.555 

Coefficients:
              Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -145.70316   18.44672  -7.899 2.53e-12 ***
Solar.R        0.05711    0.02572   2.221   0.0285 *  
Temp           2.27847    0.24600   9.262 2.22e-15 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 23.5 on 108 degrees of freedom
  (42 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.5103,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.5012 
F-statistic: 56.28 on 2 and 108 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


The summary output now includes three coefficient estimates, \(\widehat{\beta}_0, \widehat{\beta}_1, \widehat{\beta}_2\), instead of the two from simple regression. Extending the model is as straightforward as adding more variables to the formula. The derivation of the coefficient estimators is omitted here (covered in other courses), but understanding how to fit the model and interpret the output is essential.
The interpretation of the estimated coefficients is as follows (including, but not limited to the points made here):

Statistically significant positive regression coefficients indicate a positive relationship between the dependent and independent variable, while controlling for the other independent variables.

This means the estimated coefficient describes the effect that a one-unit change in the independent variable has on the dependent variable, holdingg the other independent variables constant.
For example, a variable might appear significant in a simple linear regression, but after adding another variable to the model, it may no longer be significant. In such cases, the first variable may have been a proxy for the second. After accounting for the second, the first no longer explains that much of the variation.
You’ll learn more about linear regression with multiple independent variables in other courses.

Statistically significant negative regression coefficients indicate a negative relationship in a similar manner.
Sometimes, the estimated coefficient of an independent variable is close to zero and not statistically significant. This suggests that no linear relationship exists between the dependent and independent variable, at least in the presence of the other variables.

For example, let’s extend the previous model further by including the Wind variable:

model3 <- lm(Ozone ~ Solar.R + Temp + Wind, data = airquality)
summary(model3)


Call:
lm(formula = Ozone ~ Solar.R + Temp + Wind, data = airquality)

Residuals:
    Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
-40.485 -14.219  -3.551  10.097  95.619 

Coefficients:
             Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
(Intercept) -64.34208   23.05472  -2.791  0.00623 ** 
Solar.R       0.05982    0.02319   2.580  0.01124 *  
Temp          1.65209    0.25353   6.516 2.42e-09 ***
Wind         -3.33359    0.65441  -5.094 1.52e-06 ***
---
Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1

Residual standard error: 21.18 on 107 degrees of freedom
  (42 observations deleted due to missingness)
Multiple R-squared:  0.6059,    Adjusted R-squared:  0.5948 
F-statistic: 54.83 on 3 and 107 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16


We can interpret it as follows:

The estimated model is \(\text{Ozone} = -64.34 + 0.06\cdot \text{Solar.R} + 1.65 \cdot \text{Temp} - 3.33 \cdot \text{Wind} +  \varepsilon_i\)

We notice that a one-unit change in solar radiation has a smaller estimated effect on ozone levels than a one-unit change in temperature or wind, keeping the other variables constant.

However, because these variables are measured on different scales, this comparison is not directly meaningful without standardizing the independent variables (so that they are on the same scale).


All of the independent variables are statistically significantly related to the mean ozone levels.

In addition to estimating the model and interpreting the coefficients, it is important to also evaluate how well the model describes the data. This allows us to either gain more confidence in the model, or spot possible problems in the model fit that can affect the inferences we can draw from the model fit alone. This is a very important part of any modeling task, so we’ll turn to that next.


Coefficient of determination
As linear regression is about explaining the variation in the dependent variable, it is of central importance to measure how much of that variability is explained by the independent variables in the model. The coefficient of determination, denoted as \(R^2\) and pronounced “r-squared”, tells us just this. Again, the details are covered in other courses, but we briefly introduce the key concepts. The \(R^2\) is defined as:
\[R^2 = 1- \frac{SSE}{SST} = \frac{SSM}{SST},\]
where:

\(SST\): The total sum of squares \(\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \bar{y})^2\).
\(SSE\): The residual sum of squares \(\sum_{i=1}^n (y_i - \widehat{y})^2 = \sum_{i=1}^n \widehat{\varepsilon}_i^2\)
\(SSM\): The regression sum of squares \(\sum_{i=1}^n (\widehat{y}_i - \bar{y} )^2\).

where \(y_i\) observed value of \(Y_i\), \(\widehat{y}_i\) is the fitted value for observation \(i\), and \(\bar{y}\) is the sample mean of the observed dependent variable. This statistic tells us the proportion of variation in the dependent variable that can be explained by the independent variables. When an intercept is included (and in this course we always include one), \(R^2\) is always in the range \([0,1]\) (without an intercept, it can be negative). A value of \(0\) means no variation is explained, while a value of \(1\) means all variation is explained, meaning that \(Y\) lies exactly in the column space of the independent variables. In the latter case, the lm() function will likely fit, but will issue a warning about a singular design matrix, the details of which are outside the scope of this course.
For example, consider the summary of the final model in the last section model3. It has the component r.squared:

summary(model3)$r.squared

[1] 0.6058946


This means that roughly 60% of the variation in Ozone has been accounted for by the variables Solar.R, Temp, and Wind, meaning that around 40% of its variability cannot be explained by them. You’ll learn more about how \(R^2\) is computed in the course TILM3588 Linear and Generalized Linear Models (https://opas.peppi.utu.fi/en/course/TILM3588/5071?period=2024-2027).
In addition, there are various other tools for evaluating the model fit most of which you’ll learn about in other courses!

6.1 Introduction to creating reproducible reports with RStudio

Mathematical writing with LaTeX
As a mathematical science, statistics relies on clear mathematical communication, typically involving expressions written using LaTeX, a typesetting system designed for producing technical and mathematical documents. LaTeX is built on the TeX typesetting system and provides a unified framework for mathematical notation that is difficult to express using a standard keyboard.
In statistics, such expressions include regression model equations, likelihood functions, and statistical hypotheses. In this course, we do not cover LaTeX in detail. For a more comprehensive introduction, see the course Mathematical writing (Matemaattinen kirjoittaminen) at the University of Turku. The course materials and additional resources (continuously updated) are available on the course website (in Finnish) at:
https://intranet.utu.fi/fi/yksikot/sci/yksikot/matematiikka-ja-tilastotiede/opiskelu/kurssit/Sivut/matemaattinen-kirjoittaminen.aspx
For example, a basic LaTeX command cheatsheet (in Finnish) can be found at:
https://intranet.utu.fi/fi/yksikot/sci/yksikot/matematiikka-ja-tilastotiede/opiskelu/kurssit/Documents/matkirj_latex-komentoja.pdf
For creating reproducible reports with R Markdown and Quarto, only a small subset of LaTeX is required.
Mathematical expressions are written in math mode:

Inline math: Insert the expression between the dollar sign $...$ to include it within a line of text. For example, $\pi$ is typeset as \(\pi\).
Display math: Insert the expression between double dollar signs $$...$$ or \[ ... \] to display it as a separate, centered equation.

More structured mathematical expressions can be written using environments where math mode is entered with \begin{env}, and exited via \end{env}, \begin{...} ... \end{...}. For example:

\begin{equation} ... \end{equation} produces a centered, numbered equation.
\begin{align} ... \end{align} allows multiple equations to be aligned, for example, at their equality signs.

For further details and additional LaTeX commands and environments, see the resources linked above.
Next, we introduce a typical workflow for a statistical analysis or modelling project. Such projects often combine several components, including mathematical expressions, executable code, functions defined in separate files, models estimated from data, and the interpretation and visualization of results.
This approach integrates mathematical descriptions of the (statistical) program, its actual computation, and the reporting of results within a single framework, allowing the analysis to be rerun and verified in a consistent manner.
The underlying paradigm is known as literate programming, in which the code and its explanation are developed together within the same document or project. For further details, see:
https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Literate_programming


A typical workflow for a statistical analysis/modelling project
While workflows vary across applications, most statistical projects include at least some of the following components

Problem formulation.

Specifying a research question and identifying the data required to answer it.
This is application-specific and often one of the most important stages of a statistical project.

Data collection.

Collecting that data through experiments, surveys, registers, or publicly available sources.
Data collection is often domain-specific and is not covered in detail in this course.

Data import and preprocessing.

Importing data into R, cleaning it, and performing any necessary data transformations or other data wrangling operations.
Data importing and basic preprocessing tools, such as subsetting, were covered in Module 2. This stage typically requires additional tools and techniques not covered in this course. As the old saying goes, “90% of data science is data wrangling.” (https://posit.co/blog/wrangling-unruly-data)

Model specification and estimation.

Selecting a statistical model appropriate for the research question and estimating its parameters using the collected data.
This course covered only the basics of statistical modelling. The linear regression model introduced in Module 5 is an important example and a common starting point for many statistical analyses.

Model diagnostics and validation.

Evaluating how well the model describes the data, checking its assumptions, and assessing the reliability of its results.
Model diagnostics were not covered in this course in the depth required for a comprehensive statistical analysis. However, graphical methods are often udeful for identifying potential problems, making the basic visualization skills introduced throughout this course particularly relevant.

Reporting results.

Presenting the analysis and its results using tables, figures and explanatory text.
In R, results can be displayed using functions such as summary(model), while objects and outputs can be saved for later use with functions such as write.csv() or saveRDS().

Interpretation and conclusions.

Interpreting the statistical results in the context of the original research question.
What do the results tell us about the phenomenon being studied? What conclusions can be drawn, and what limitations should be acknowledged?


The above workflow is typically iterative, meaning that results from later stages often lead to revisiting the earlier steps. For example, model diagnostics may reveal problems that require additional data preprocessing or changes to the model specification.
The desired outcome is often a report that clearly communicates what was done, why it was done, and how it was done. Ideally, another person should be able to understand the analysis and reproduce its results using the same data and code.
Many of these steps can be combined into a single reproducible document containing explanatory text and executable code. Larger projects may also rely on separate scripts, functions, and data files. In either case, the goal is to make the connection between the statistical analysis and its reported results transparent and reproducible.
Next, we introduce reporting tools available in RStudio that support this approach.


Reproducible documents with Quarto

Quarto Documents
Quarto is an open-source scientific and technical publishing system developed by Posit PBC (formerly RStudio). It is considered as the multilingual, next-generation successor to R Markdown, which is still available and widely used and which we’ll introduce briefly after covering Quarto. Quarto has many new features and capabilities and is a modern and widely used tool for creating reproducible documents describing statistical analysis and modeling projects.
Quarto allows the user to combine plain text, mathematical notation with LaTeX, and executable code chunks that support a wide variety of programming languages (incl. Python). It is therefore an example of literate programming, as both the analytical results and their implementation in code can be described with a single narrative document. This allows researchers to describe the abstract statistical and mathematical concepts employed in the analysis, while presenting their programmatic implementation simultaneously.
Quarto can be used to create and publish a wide variety of different reproducible documents, such as research articles, presentations (slideshows), dashboards, websites, blogs, books (the material for this course is created as a Quarto book), and research reports. It is built on Pandoc markdown (https://pandoc.org/) and therefore it is easy to include mathematical notation with LaTeX, which is useful for statistical projects.

Quarto - Creating a document
A Quarto document can be created by selecting File –> New File –> Quarto Document in RStudio. The following window opens:

Here, you can select the document type (Document, Presentation, Interactive) on the left, and give the title and author details, as well as select the preferred output format. After selecting these, clicking Create generates an empty .qmd file.
A .qmd file can then be rendered to become another file, which is of the selected format. The document is executed from top to bottom when rendered. This shows that a single source file can be rendered into multiple output formats including .html, .pdf, and a .docx file. For R code, Quarto uses the knitr package to execute code chunks.


Quarto - Structure of a document
Once you have created the empty Quarto document it should look like this

The top line contains buttons for various specifications, of which the most important are the blue arrow with the text Render and the green square with C and a plus sign. The latter can be used to insert a code chunk corresponding to different languages. The former renders the quarto document to either .pdf or a .html file, which creates a new local file with the contents given in the body of the file (empty after initializing), formatted as dictated by the contents of the YAML located at the top of the file between the two --- delimiters. That is, a Quarto document consists of two main parts detailed below.

YAML
Every Quarto document begins with a YAML front matter, which is a human-readable configuration format located at the top of the document. This is automatically generated when you create a Quarto document, and often does not require any modifications, but below we go through the basic arguments that you can include to make the document more informative.

title: the title of the document, e.g., “Modeling Project”.
author: the author(s) of the document.
date: rather self-explanatory.
format: the output format of the document.

html: output displayed in a web browser.
pdf: output is a standard PDF-file.


An example of an YAML header is given below:

The selection format: html will generate a html file that looks like this in the browser:

In contrast, the selection format: pdf generates a pdf file that looks like this:



Body
This is where the contents of the file should be. It obeys the conventional Markdown formatting, of which you can learn more here:
https://quarto.org/docs/authoring/markdown-basics.html
Markdown is a plain text format that is designed to be easy to write and easy to read. Despite this, it is extremely flexible and can be used to create impressive documents without relying on graphical user interfaces that are common for typical software used to edit, e.g., Word files. Markdown can be considered as a plain text alternative to conventional text editing software.
Below, we cover the most important elements of Markdown syntax.



Quarto - Markdown basics
Quarto uses the Pandoc variation of markdown as the underlying document syntax. Originally, Markdown was a text-to-HTML conversion tool, that is, it takes text written in plain text and converts it into HTML-code, removing the need to learn to “code” with HTML. For further information, see:
https://daringfireball.net/projects/markdown/
As a plain text formatting system, Markdown leverages simple characters to format text, basics of which are outlined below.

Text formatting and headings
In typical text editing software, the appearance of text can be modified in various ways. For example, you can bold, italicize, or both, to highlight certain parts of your text. In Markdown, you get italicized or bold text by inserting the text between one or two asterisks. For example, *this* is rendered as this, and similarly **this** gets rendered to this.
Strikethrough is achieved by enclosing text between two tildes on each side, for example ~~like this~~. The previous is possible due to the inline code formatting, which is achieved by enclosing text between single back ticks, for example `like this`. This is not, however, supported by the ViLLE platform, so the above will likely appear just as bolded text.
It is necessary, typically, to divide the text to different sections, separated by section titles. In Markdown, sections are created by inserting # in front of the section title on a new line. Further hierarchy, subsections etc., is achieved by inserting more hash signs:

# Heading 1: largest
## Heading 2: second largest
### Heading 3: third largest
#### Heading 4: …
Up to level 6 headings.



Lists
Lists are used to organize content into structured bullet points or ordered steps. The above unordered bullet list is an example. Such lists can be created by inserting -, *, or + as the first character of a new line, and repeating it for each of the items:
- First item
- Second item
- Third item
The above gets rendered as:

First item
Second item
Third item

Similarly, ordered lists are created by using numbers:
1. First item
2. Second item
3. Third item
which gets rendered as

First item
Second item
Third item

Lists can be nested by using indentation (pressing Tab):
- Main item
  - Sub-item 1
  - Sub-item 2
- Second item
Is rendered as:

Main item

Sub-item 1
Sub-item 2

Second item

Lists are useful for various use cases, such as presenting steps in an analysis, summarizing results, or presenting the structure of the report.


Equations
Mathematical expressions can be written using LaTeX syntax, as introduced earlier. Inline equations are written between single dollar signs $...$, for example $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x$ is rendered inline as \(y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x\).
Displayed equations (centered on a new line, set off by extra space above and below) are written using double dollar signs $$...$$. For example:
$$
y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x
$$
is rendered as \[ y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 x \]
Displayed equations are useful for presenting models, formulas, or longer expressions clearly within the text. More advanced expressions can be written using LaTeX environments such as equation, align, or cases, as discussed earlier and for which you can see the provided resources.


Code chunks
One of the main reasons for using Quarto (or different Markdown versions) is the ability to include executable code chunks directly within the document. They are pieces of code that are run and displayed in the document, so the document can then use the objects created with the code. For example, if I include a code chunk

x <- rnorm(1)

The object x is available to subsequent R code chunks and inline R expressions during the same rendering process. This means that, for example, I can include results directly within the text by using the inline code

The value of `x` is `r x`.

which renders to
The value of x is -0.0236589.
The value of x changes whenever I render the document since I have not set a seed number. This ensures that whatever is reported in the rendered document is always consistent with the underlying analysis.
To include a code chunk like the one above, we can write
```{r}
x <- rnorm(1)
```
That is, enclosing it between two lines with three backticks (`), or by pressing the green square with “C” in it on the top panel, which is short for “chunk”, and selecting R.
The behavior of the included code chunks can be controlled using different options. For example, writing
{r, echo = FALSE} x <- rnorm(1)
hides the code chunk, but runs the code and shows the output if the code chunk prints something. In contrast, writing eval = FALSE, would show the code but not run it. For further options, see:
https://quarto.org/docs/computations/execution-options.html#output-options



Quarto - Output and rendering options
Quarto provides several options for customizing the appearance of documents through settings defined in the YAML front matter. For example, you can include a .css file that gives you complete control of what the .html files look like, as well as a preamble.tex file that you can use to modify the LaTeX commands and styles in any way you want.
For less involved modifications, Quarto has different premade themes that you can choose. For example, to define separate themes for light and dark mode for a HTML-document, we can write
---
title: "Dark mode"
format: 
  html:
    theme:
      light: flatly
      dark: darkly
---
That automatically inserts a toggle in the generated HTML-file that allows the user to switch between a light and a dark theme, as shown below:
The light theme:

and the dark theme:

Quarto supports a wide range of additional output formats and customization options. In addition, it supports interactive documents that can be published online and allow user interaction.
For most statistical reports, such as course assignments, PDF output is often required, although a HTML output is at times accepted as well. Familiarity with Quarto (or R Markdown, introduced next) provides a useful framework for structuring and writing reproducible reports and can be used for, e.g., course assignments, exercises, and documenting your own projects.



R Markdown
R Markdown documents (.Rmd) can be considered as a predecessor to Quarto documents. The core idea of Literate Programming is the same: combining text, code, and results within a single document.
Quarto is a more recent and general framework that extends this approach to multiple programming languages and output formats. While R Markdown is primarily designed for use with R, it also supports other languages through additional tools.
Quarto can also render most .Rmd files, although this is not its primary use case. R Markdown remains widely used and provides an alternative for creating reproducible documents based on the same underlying principles.

6.2 Structuring an analysis project
A statistical analysis or modelling project typically consists of multiple components. These include the data and the code used to analyze it as well as the outputs generated and the final report that combines all of these. Therefore, it is of central importance to organize these components in a clear and consistent way so that the project is easy to understand, reproduce, and collaborate on. This ensures that other people (such as your colleagues, supervisors (bosses), or co-authors) can also run the same analysis and understand what is happening.

Project structure
A common way to organize a project on your computer is as follows:
project/
  data/
  R/
  scripts/
  output/
  report/
where each line corresponds to a folder and indentation means that the folder belongs to the folder at the previous indentation level. Here:

data/: raw or processed data files.
R/: helper functions and/or other reusable code.
scripts/: analysis scripts specific to this project.
output/: figures, tables, and other generated results.
report/: the final report (e.g., Quarto or R Markdown document)

This separation helps keep the project organized and makes it easier to understand and reproduce the analysis. For example, with this structure, you could simply zip the folder project/ and share it with a colleague or a friend, and they could simply run the analysis themselves, provided that the folder is self-contained.


R Projects in RStudio
Using an RStudio Project makes it easier to organize all files related to an analysis within a single directory. That is, you can create an RStudio Project directly into the project/ folder above, and that folder is automatically set as the working directory, which simplifies file management and improves reproducibility.
To create an RStudio Project you can click the icon with the cube with an R inside it:

or, click File –> New Project. Both open the New Project Wizard window:

Where you can either create a new directory (a new project folder), or select an existing directory, if, for example, you already have the data stored somewhere on your computer. Here, we create a new directory, after which we need to choose the Project Type:

Here, we already see the wide range of use cases that RStudio covers. In this brief tutorial, we will select New Project:

Next, you can select a name for the project folder and where it should exist on your local computer. Additional selections include creating a Git repository and using renv for the project. The former is briefly discussed below, while the latter is outside the scope of this course.
After clicking Create Project, the root directory for the project is created. Now the newly created directory is the working directory for the project, and in the bottom-right panel you see its contents (which initially contains the project configuration file):

Note that the file path will be different for different users, and here the example_project was created as a subfolder of the project folder where the author stores all files corresponding to this course. You can create new folders by clicking on the folder with the green/white plus sign on the top left.

File paths and portability
When an RStudio Project is opened, its root directory is normally set as the working directory. This means that files within the project can be accessed using file paths relative to that directory. For example, suppose we create a script named example_source.R in the folder scripts/, containing only print(rnorm(100)). We can then execute the script using the function source() from the project root. For example, running the following command in another script:

source("scripts/example_source.R")

By running this line, 100 realizations from a standard normal distribution are printed to the console.
Note that relative paths are always interpreted with respect to the current working directory. This may differ depending on how the code is executed. For example, Quarto documents are normally rendered using the document’s own directory as the working directory.
Therefore, it is advised to not hard-code full file paths into the project, as those differ between your and your colleagues’ computers. In the above example, and on the author’s computer, the following also works:
source("/Users/admin/Documents/R-kurssi/example_project/Example project/scripts/example_source.R")
But it will fail if you zip the contents of this project, send it to your friend, and they store it in a folder titled project_with_friend/. The first example, in contrast, uses a relative file path, defined with respect to the current working directory. When working from the project root, the relative path remains valid even if the entire project is moved to another location.
The function getwd() can be used to get the current working directory, which can be useful for understanding how file paths work. The here() function from the package here can also be used to construct paths relative to the project root in a robust way. You can find further details with the command ?here::here().



Reproducibility practices
The following practices help to produce reproducible analysis that yields the same results even on other machines (e.g., another person’s computer)

Use set.seed() when working with simulations or random processes to recreate a certain realization.
Avoid hard-coded file paths as discussed above, and use relative paths instead.
Render the full report regularly to ensure that all code runs from start to finish.
Record session information with sessionInfo() to document the R version, loaded packages and their, versions and the computing environment.

Differences in R or package versions between computers may lead to errors or differences in results.
For more advanced projects, tools such as renv can be used to manage project-specific package dependencies.


The goal should be that another user can run the entire project from a clean environment on another machine and obtain the same results.

6.3 Version control
This section is a brief introduction on how to connect RStudio to Git and GitHub. Version control with Git and GitLab is covered in more detail in other courses (basic computer science classes), so we will not discuss its underlying concepts here. Instead, this section provides a brief practical introduction to connecting RStudio Projects to GitHub and managing project versions directly from RStudio.
For an introduction to Git concepts and terminology, see Some Git basics – Happy Git and GitHub for the useR.
We will only cover using GitHub for personal project version control and storage, and not discuss in detail how to use it for collaborative work.
While there are many ways to connect an RStudio Project with GitHub, we will consider a relatively straightforward approach. The steps are as follows:

Have Git installed and a registered GitHub account.
Connect Git, GitHub, and RStudio via HTTPS authentication (Personal Access Token (PAT)).
Initialize a repository on GitHub in your browser.
Create a new R Project and select Version Control and select Git.
Paste the URL of the repository created in step 2. and create a local directory for it.
Create the project


Register a GitHub account and install Git
Install Git by following the instructions in:
https://git-scm.com/install/
Register a GitHub account at:
https://github.com/signup


Connect Git, GitHub, and RStudio
To perform authenticated Git operations with GitHub, such as pushing changes, you need to configure authentication. Common options include SSH keys and HTTPS authentication using a Personal Access Token (PAT). This is, however, explained better here:
https://happygitwithr.com/connect-intro
Using an HTTPS PAT is encouraged at this point.
After you have established this connection, everything should work seamlessly and effortlessly. We will recreate the Connect to GitHub example from the above link, but do it entirely in RStudio instead of using Git in the shell.


Initialize a repository on your GitHub account in browser

Go to github.com and to the Repositories tab.
Click the green button with the text New, and give your repository a name and a description (optional). Toggle the Add README button on.
Now you should see a repository with only the file README.md.

Note that the README.md is also a markdown document. Next, we connect RStudio to clone the GitHub repository to our local computer, creating a local copy of the repository and its contents, including the README.md file.


Creating a new R Project and connecting it to the GitHub repository
Next, follow the same instructions as before to create a new R Project, summarized below:

Select File
Select New Project
Select Version Control from the New Project Wizard
Select Git and paste the URL of your repository (it should be of the form github.com//.git, for example, https://github.com/johnsnow/linear_regression_project.git) (we use HTTPS cloning here).

(*If in step 4. above the Git selection is not available, you may want to restart RStudio and try again. If that does not help, see tips here: https://happygitwithr.com/rstudio-see-git#rstudio-see-git)
Now, if you previously connected RStudio to Git, a new project should open with the README.md file in the file tree (that is, on your local computer). Open the README.md file in RStudio.
The file should contain the name of your repository as a Markdown heading, such ase # linear_regression_project. You can also add a short description of the project below the heading. Compare this to the file on your GitHub profile and ensure that they match. Now, write something on a new line in the file and save it (either by File –> Save or by pressing CTRL + S)
Next, to ensure that the linking between RStudio and GitHub works correctly, select the Git tab in the top right panel. Select the files you wish to commit and click Commit, which opens up a commit window, where you specify the commit message and finally push the files to the remote repository with the green arrow icon.
You might be prompted to authenticate using your PAT which you should do. Now head back to the repository in GitHub and open the README.md file. Ensure that the file now contains the lines you inserted. If it does, you have successfully created a commit locally and pushed it to your GitHub repository.
All of this language might seem odd at this point. A few explanations are given below:

What are local and remote repositories and how do they differ? A local repository is the version of the project stored on your own computer, where you make changes and create commits. A remote repository is a copy of the project hosted on a server, such as GitHub. The two are not automatically synchronized. You use push to send changes to the remote repository and pull to retrieve updates from it.
What is a commit? A commit is a snapshot of the entire project (or selected file(s)) at a given point in time. It records the current state of the files along with a short message describing the changes. Each commit records a version of the project that can be inspected or revisited later.
What does it mean to “push” to a remote repository? When you make commits locally on your computer, they are stored only in your local repository (folder). Pushing sends these committed changes to a remote repository, such as GitHub, so they are stored there and available to others (or to yourself on another machine).

The material presented in this section provides only a brief introduction. You will develop a deeper understanding through practice as you work on your own projects and studies. Version control allows you to track, store, and synchronize different versions of your work across time and across machines. When combined with a remote repository hosted on GitHub, version control also provides an additional copy of your committed project files, alongside a platform for managing and sharing projects. For example, repositories hosted on platforms such as GitHub can be used to document your work and showcase your skills.

6.4 Additional tools

Modern R workflows

The tools introduced in this course are primarily part of “base R”. Another popular approach to statistical programming and data science uses the tidyverse collection of packages, which is particularly useful for data wrangling and visualization.

Tidyverse is a collection of R packages for data manipulation, visualization and analysis with a focus on readable code and efficient data processing and analysis pipelines.
You’ll learn tidyverse-based programming in a future course (TILM3708 Statistical Programming and Visualisation, https://opas.peppi.utu.fi/en/course/TILM3708/100873?period=2024-2027)




Data sources and acquisition

Parallel and high performance computing for R

Many computations in R are executed sequentially, meaning that they use only one processor core at a time. However, certain packages and numerical libraries can already utilize multiple processor cores.

Parallel copmuting allows suitable computational tasks to be distributed across multiple processor cores, potentially reducing computation time.
This is particularly useful for simulation studies, repeated model estimation, and other computationally intensive statistical tasks.
R provides several tools and packages for parallel computing, including the built-in parallel package.
Different parallelization packages are often specific to a certain operating system.

High-performance computing (HPC) refers to the use of powerful computing systems, such as supercomputers, to perform computationally demanding tasks.

Supercomputes typically contain large numbers of processor cores and substantial computational resources, allowing researchers to perform analyses that would be impractical on an ordinary personal computer.
In Finland, CSC provides high-performance computing services for research, including access to supercomputers such as Roihu and LUMI.
Learn more at: https://csc.fi/
Yet another good reason to learn computational statistics and consider a career in scientific research!




Automating repetitive tasks with R

One of the major advantages of programming is the ability to automate repetitive and time-consuming tasks.

For example, R scripts can be used to automatically retrieve new data, perform statistical analyses, and generate updated figures and reports.
Quarto documents, including dashboards, can combine these operations into a reproducible reporting workflow.
To run these workflows automatically at specified intervals, an external scheduling tool or service is required. For example, Posit Connect or GitHub Actions can be used to schedule the execution and rendering of Quarto reports.
This makes its possible to create reports and dashboards that are updated regularly without manually rerunning the analysis.

For example, you could create a dashboard that tracks economic variables or news on topics of interest.

An R script could retrieve new data from an online source, process it, and generate updated visualizations.
By scheduling the execution of the script and rendering of the Quarto document, the published dashboard could be updated automatically every day or week.
